title: Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 DENTON — Children gathered at the Wharves of Choptank Visitor & Heritage Center on Saturday for an afternoon full of crafts, wooden toys, painting and more as the holidays quickly approach.In an event put on by the Caroline County Council of Arts and The Foundry, its art gallery, children were welcomed to build their own toys, greet Santa and meet the Grinch. Two more Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits Saturdays are scheduled: Dec. 14 and Dec. 21 from noon to 4 p.m.
Caroline County Council of Arts Executive Director George Karos said the event is a "fun way to celebrate the holidays."
"Everyone can make art and spend time with loved ones — especially a win-win as proceeds go towards supporting local youth programs and spreading holiday cheer," Karos said in an emailed statement.
Megan Krizovensky, program manager for Caroline County Council of Arts, said in an interview that last weekend's event was a success. It's the first time the art organization put on Santa's Workshop.
"It was pretty good," Krizovenksy said of Saturday's turnout. "I know the first week we expected to be a little slower. But we actually had at least 50 children there, and we were prepared for over 100. So we're hoping that (Dec. 14 and Dec. 21) can pick it up much bigger just for the kid's sake."
Last Saturday, the Chesapeake Culinary Center participated in the event and donated cookies and cocoa. Krizovenksy said Earth Tones Cafe will be donating food for this Saturday.
Additionally, students from Caroline County Public Schools are volunteering, gaining student service learning hours. The first-time event runs fully on donations, Krizovenksy added.
"The event is completely donation-based with all proceeds going to support local youth programs through the Caroline County Council of Arts," she said.
Krizovensky said local artist Steve Mead, formerly the board treasurer for the arts council, was integral in the event's formulation.
The hope is that Santa's Workshop can continue in the future, with some of this year's proceeds working to fund a second annual Santa's Workshop. Registration is free with a suggested donation of $15 per child.
"The goal is to create a magical experience for kids who otherwise might not have a great holiday," Krizovenksy said. "We want to make sure that it's free. Our mission is to enrich the community through the arts, and Caroline County itself is a unique place anyway with a lot of deep-rooted tradition. So we're trying to create authentic experiences that reflect and celebrate the spirit of that community."
To register for Dec. 14 or Dec. 21, sign up at carolinearts.org/events/santas-workshop-in-the-island-of-misfit-toys/ or visit The Foundry Art Gallery at 401 Market St. in Denton.

title: Federalsburg unveils sign to recognize historic 2023 election, people who made it possible
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Federalsburg unveils sign to recognize historic 2023 election, people who made it possible

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 744
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Rev. Jeffrey Butler, a Federalsburg resident, remembers when Brooklyn Avenue went from being a dirt road to a paved one in the late 1970s. He also remembers the more than 40 years it took for the town to get that road repaved."It was so bad," he said. "I mean, just tearing cars up. And we went to the town to complain. They still didn't do nothing."
"Finally, along with this lawsuit, came them also fixing this road up after 40 years," Butler said.
Since a lawsuit led to the election of the town's first two Black council members last year, the road — which is situated in a historically Black area in town — has been repaved.
On Saturday, with the newly paved Brooklyn Avenue in view, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner and the Federalsburg Town Council unveiled a new sign that commemorates the town's historic election and the new election system that made it possible.
The sign recognizes the individuals and groups who helped make it possible for Black Councilwomen Darlene Pitt Hammond and Brandy James to be elected to the Town Council in September 2023.
A MARKER OF PROGRESSAfter the unveiling, Hammond looked at the sign, tears forming in her eyes.
"It's a lot," she said, taking a pause, "to think that this small little town was able to stand for the rights of all people, not some people."
Hammond, who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit against the town, said the progress that has been made in the town is "heartwarming" and "breathtaking."
"It's a dream come true for me and for others that (came) before me, that we have established that everybody should be represented no matter what the color of your skin is," she said.
Although Black residents now make up nearly half of the town's population, the town had never had a minority representative on the council in its 200-year history. In June 2023 — through charter amendments, legislation and federal court rulings — the town's at-large election system was changed to a two-district system to ensure more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.
In April, a $260,000 settlement was reached in the lawsuit filed against the town by the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, the Caucus of African American Leaders and Federalsburg residents regarding its discriminatory election system.
The settlement included a sweeping array of measures aimed at providing reconciliation after the town's previous election system was determined to have prevented Black residents from electing their chosen representatives. This includes the town apologizing to those who brought on the lawsuit, affixing a plaque to its town hall building, proclaiming Sept. 26 as Voting Rights Day and erecting the historical marker in the town's Black community.
Hammond said this sign unveiling and the first annual Voting Rights Day celebration, which was held in September, point to "a new era" in Federalsburg.
"It is a new era where everybody has a voice and everybody will be heard," she said.
After years of Butler speaking out about the need for Brooklyn Avenue to be repaved, Hammond said the new council was able to get the project done in about a year.
Before the sign was unveiled, Mayor Kim Abner said she and the council are excited about the direction that Federalsburg is going in.
"We have great things to come," she said. "We are making great progress in the town, and we are super excited that you're all here to celebrate."
Butler said he is hopeful more positive changes are coming with the current council in place.
"It's coming," he said. "We know Rome wasn't built in a day, so it's coming."
Sherone Lewis, a Federalsburg native and first vice president for the Caroline County branch of the NAACP who was a plaintiff on the lawsuit, called it surreal to be celebrating the changes that have been made.
"But I must say, the struggle continues," she said. "We still have a lot of work to do for diversity, equity and inclusion. I know those are buzz words these days. But I do believe that because I want this for my children, my grandchildren."
Willie Woods, president of the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, said the new sign is something that will be seen and read for generations.
"I hate to talk about it from this standpoint, but in the future, we will be passed on and there will be other generations," she said. "And this signage will remind them of the stance that was taken and of the progress that Federalsburg has embraced as we are moving forward."

title: Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Read News Document

 It wasn't a prediction.It was just something Mike Kern believed.
"If we can get out of the region, I think we have a good shot at states," Kern said of Queen Anne's County High's girls soccer team.
That was at the outset of the season. The Lions did get out of the region, then went on to become the first Bayside Conference school ever to win a girls state soccer championship.
Now, as the girls basketball season approaches tip-off, Kern again strongly believes if Queen Anne's can get out of its region, it has a chance to do well at the state level.
"We're very multi-dimensional," Kern said. "All of our guards can penetrate and shoot. And then our post players are very dangerous inside. They move well. They're very athletic. So I think the sky's the limit for them. The biggest thing is play as a team. We learned that in soccer. If we play as a team and aren't selfish, and do the little things, I think we can do really well."
Getting out of the Class 2A East Region II could prove more difficult than in soccer. Kent Island still has Sydney Riska and Lacey Dauses. Wicomico returns the bulk of the team that handed the Lions their only three losses last season, including bouts for the Bayside Conference and 2A East Region II championships. And Parkside has improved.
But this Queen Anne's team is different.
Not only does Kern return the majority of a team that went 20-3 and won the North Bayside championship, he welcomes two additions who have the potential to be impact players in juniors Damya Henry, a transfer from Cambridge-South Dorchester, and Cheyanne Hollis — daughter of Queen Anne's boys head coach Jeff Hollis — who has been sidelined by injury the past two seasons.
"With our core coming back, plus those additions, I think we stand a good chance of challenging them this year," Kern said of Wicomico. "Damya gives us that defensive pressure. She reads well. Anticipates well. And she's quick. So she definitely helps on the defensive end.
"And Chayenne, she's a true post player; and that will free up Bea (Holthaus) and Lucy (Taylor) a little bit having her in there," Kern continued.
Then there's the core group. Seniors RJ Ensor and Lucy Taylor return along with sophomores Laila Coles, Kariana Hickson, and Holthaus, the 2023 North Bayside Player of the Year.
"The thing about our team right now, I feel like we can score so many different ways," Kern said. "We have pretty good shooters. We can get the ball inside. We can drive. We're a very multi-dimensional team. And Bea herself is very multi-dimensional. She can play outside, go inside. She can drive.
"I'm not worried about us being able to score this year," Kern added. "My biggest focus so far is making sure we play good defense. One of the things that we've done well over the years is we've been a really good defensive team. And I feel like we have so much energy on the offense, that we kind of rest on the defense. And we can't do that with good teams. So we have to play up-tempo defense the entire game."
Kent Island remains Queen Anne's biggest challenger, though Cambridge-SD, with the senior core of Le'Asia Todd, Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin have the potential to give Queen Anne's a battle.
Here's a look at this season's teams.
CAMBRIDGE-SD
Head Coach: Shamya Johnson.
Who's Where: Le'Asia Todd (Sr., C); Destiny Johnson (Sr., G); Tejanae Ballin (Sr., PG); AzEyera Johnson (Sr., F); Skyla Ali (So., F); Jade Ballin (So., F); JaNaya Stanley (Jr., G); Tonyia Brooks (Sr., G); Aamiyah Wilcox (Sr., C); Neveah Adams (Fr., G); Montiasha Jackson (So., G); Amari Winters (Fr., F/C); Kennedy Bourne (So., F); Kamryn Bourne (So., F); D'Asia Mack (So., G).
Outlook: Todd can reach 1,000 career points in Thursday's opener against Crisfield, and together with Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin makes the Vikings a favorite in 1A East Region II.
And though Coach Johnson thinks Cambridge-SD can again reach the 1A state quarterfinals, one of her biggest challenges is keeping her team's intensity and discipline up from start to finish.
"That was the conversation we had tonight,' Coach Johnson said Tuesday in a phone interview. "'You all got it. You've got the pieces. But you all don't have the discipline. And that's the difference.'"
Johnson also knows her team needs to play great transition defense and create points off turnovers if it hopes to challenge Queen Anne's and Kent Island.
COL. RICHARDSON
Head Coach: Tom Corsey.
Who's Where: Jaz Jackson (Jr., G); Monae Ross (Sr., C); Selina Austriville (So., F); Tybria Williams (Sr., G); Ella Downie (So., F); Angelina Algre (Fr., C).
Outlook: Corsey thinks the 6-foot-5 Algre can develop into an inside force.
"She's a work in progress," Corsey said. "She's a presence. She's learning, but I'm going to get her there."
This is one of the younger teams Corsey's coached, but the goal is another 10-win season with eyes on upsetting a 2A school.
EASTON
Head Coach: Lesley Staehli.
Who's Where: Sam Murphy (Sr., G); Serenity Velez (Jr., G); Maia Bailey (Fr., G); Ki'Mauri Lewis (So., G); Jordyn Wilson-Colbert (So., F/C); Myles Booker (Sr., F/C); Dakota Dietrich (Sr., G); Addison Knox (So., G/F); Stella Kabler (Jr., G); Taylor Bowen (Fr., F/C); Addison Chandler (Sr., G/F).
Outlook: The Warriors are an interesting mix.
Velez returns as one of the team's top scorers, and Murphy has transferred from Saints Peter and Paul.
"She is one of the scrappiest people I have ever played against the last four years that I've been coaching defense wise," Staehli said of Murphy. "Now it's awesome to have her with us because she barely comes out."
Bailey, daughter of Marty Bailey, who has come over from the boys team to be an assistant, could be one of the Bayside's top newcomers. And then there is a list of talent that includes Knox, Kabler and Bowen, who helped the Warriors reach the state field hockey semifinals this past season, and Chandler, a force on the Easton soccer team.
"We're going to be fast," Staehli said. "Everybody has talent. I think we're going to shock a lot of people this year with the fact (they're) not expecting a lot of athletic people to come back into the program with us having no jayvee last year. There's certain teams we'll struggle with, but I think we're going to be pretty good."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Tyray Johnson.
Who's Where: Kate Cannon (Sr., C); Talicia Wright (So., PG); Jane Cleary (So., F); Love Jackson (Jr., SF); Kaliyah Smith (Sr., SF); Ariyana Green (So., SF); Saniyah Jones (So., C); Tameeia Savage (Jr., SF); Juliette Camilli (Jr., SG); Sanorra Parker (Fr., SG); Abigael Lachance (Sr., SF); Emerence Boutaud (Jr., PF).
Outlook: Johnson begins his fourth season with the biggest roster he's ever had at Kent with 12. Though still young, experience was gained last year, especially with Wright, who returns at point guard.
"We turned the ball over a lot last year," Johnson said. "She (Wright) stepped up toward the end of the season. So a lot of the mistakes she made early on we won't really have them this year. So it's going to be less turnovers for us."
Speed and defense will be critical if the undersized Trojans are to improve on last season's five-win mark.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Dave Plumer.
Who's Where: Sydney Riska (Sr., F); Lacey Dauses (Jr., G); Abigail Staton (Sr., PG); Ellie Burnside (Sr., G); Machaela Thomas (So., C); Avery Eaton (Sr., G)
Outlook: Lilli Dauses graduated and Makayla Kropfelder transferred to Broadneck. But don't expect the Bucs to fall far from the top.
The smooth-playing Riska was a double-double machine last season, and Lacey Dauses gained confidence with her ability to attack the rim and draw contact. Add Thomas, a 6-foot-2 center, who could create problems for opponents, and Burnside, the first player off the bench from last season.
"I think Lacey had grown as a player and in size," Plumer said. "Obviously Sydney had a big year last year, and now adding another 6-2 center to play along side of her is going to benefit her as well. Who are you going to guard? Machaela's got great footwork. She just needs playing time to get better.
"I think we got to run," Plumer continued. "I mean we're guard heavy. We do have a big player inside but I think we're going to be a running team. We just got to play. There's talent there. It's going to take them a month or two to get them up to speed. But they can play."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: AJ Jackson.
Who's Where: Taryn Brandt (Sr., G); Jasiyah Henry (Sr., G); Emma Keating (Sr., F); Ashley Kercheval (Sr., F); Megan Rogers (Sr., G); Kaitlyn Thompson (Sr., C); Sarah Brown (Sr., G); MyKira Allen (Jr., F); Yariah Dowell (Jr., G); Irma Sanchez (Jr., G); Nevaeh Irby (So., G).
Outlook: The Bulldogs lost the majority of their scoring from last season with the graduation of Precious Phillips, Chloe Escoe, Ashleigh Lawry and first-team all-North Bayside pick Selaya Garrison.
Jackson will lean heavily on Henry, a four-year varsity starter, for scoring, along with Keating and Dowell.
"Getting back to the fundamentals," Jackson said Caroline's key to success. "Rebounding, boxing out, good passes. The basics. So far I've loved what I've seen in preseason. The girls are buying in. There are some things we need to improve on, but the girls are working hard."
NORTH DORCHESTER
Head Coach: Dontele Pinder.
Who's Where: Remedy Wongus (So., G/F); Areinya Taylor (Sr., G); Ziya Patton (Sr., F); Diamond Newbill (Fr., G); Sammir Holland (Fr., G); Destiny Wongus (Fr., G).
Outlook: An assistant at Colonel Richardson the past eight seasons, Pinder begins his first head coaching job with plenty of optimism.
"I feel like we have a great core group," Pinder said. "We're kind of in the middle of the transition, where we have some of our key seniors that are leading, but we have a good group of freshmen that I feel like are going to be productive in the beginning. I'm excited and I think they're excited about the change. Hopefully we can make some noise here in the North."
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Mike Kern.
Who's Where: Damya Henry (Jr., G); Cheyanne Hollis (Jr., F/C); Bea Holthaus (So., F); Laila Coles (So., G); Kariana Hickson (So., G); Taylor Jordan (So., G); RJ Ensor (Sr., G); Lucy Taylor (Sr., C); Sydney Pinder (Jr., F); Keilah Reed (Jr., G); Abby Robinson (So., G); Dillon Simpler (So., G); Lex Kern (So., G).
Outlook: With practically everyone back from last season, as well as the additions of Hollis and Henry, it's not surprising Kern thinks the potential is there to do well at the state level, if Queen Anne's can advance out of the region.
"We've never had a team that can all shoot," Kern said. "We've had teams where we had one true shooter and that's it. We might have a kid who could drive. We had Kendall Moxey (Queen Anne's career leading scorer) who could play the post. But we've never had a solid (team) that can shoot from so many different area's of the court."
That's a combination that could have the Lions driving deep into another postseason.
ST. MICHAELS
Head Coach: Jonathan Matthews.
Who's Where: Jordyn Beckett (So., F/C); Hanna Corkran (So., F/C); Aleah George (So., F); Rebeca Martinez (Jr., G); Evelyn Mautz (Fr., G); Kayla Montoya (So. SG); Olivia Patrick (Jr., G/F); Alayna Porter (Fr., G); Maddisyn Roe (Jr., G); Bella Simmons (Fr., G); Kendall Rosenberger (So., C); Tess Weller (Jr., PG); Shayla Frink (Jr., C); Kaelyn Hicks (Fr., G/F); Maleia Loffland (Fr., G).
Outlook: Another former Colonel Richardson assistant, Matthews begins his first head coaching job hoping to build on what former head coach Mark Potter started.
"Mark gave us a good start from last year for the ninth graders that are 10th graders this year," Matthews said. "We're still working on some of our developmental things, but I think in the long run we'll be all right. I have high hopes for them."
SAINTS PETER & PAUL
Head Coach: Katie Murphy.
Who's Where: Avery McCall (Jr., F/C); Annie Albright (Jr., G); Lucy Rankin (Jr., G/F); Hazel Spurry (Jr., G); Emma Hainey (So., G); Kaylin Palmer (So., F/C); Bridget Gilman (So., G); Tara Foley (So., G/F); Ryleigh Briddell (So., C/F); Veronica Pool (So., G); Natalee Lyons (Fr., G); Caroline Jallade (Fr., C/F).
Outlook: While the Sabres and Delmarva Christian have met for the Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference title the last three seasons, Murphy thinks this season could be more wide open with Worcester Prep, Gunston and Salisbury School pushing to improve.
"Everyone is a threat," Murphy said.
Murphy admits it's been somewhat hard to gauge her team's potential because she hasn't had her full lineup for games or practices.
And though the losses of Morgan Quade (graduation) and Sam Murphy (transfer) will hurt, the Sabres have a solid core with McCall, Albright, Rankin, Hainey and the continuing emergence of Palmer and Gilman.
"We finally have everybody back and we're working on a few things to find out who those (starting) five are," Murphy said. "They want to learn. They want to get better. Working together as a team is where we are right now."

title: Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster
author: David Harsanyi
content:
Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: David Harsanyi | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 640
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kevin McCarthy has become the first House speaker to ever be successfully ousted in a motion to vacate vote. One day, you can tell your grandchildren you were alive to witness this completely pointless bit of history.Rep. Matt Gaetz's (R-Fla.) self-aggrandizing political stunt makes no sense and changes nothing - other than perhaps his fundraising totals.And other than some platitudinous blathering about "the establishment" and "the uniparty," I still haven't seen anyone offer a coherent reason - not even retroactively - for how any of this is the "best way to advance the conservative agenda." It would be one thing, perhaps an admirable thing, if Gaetz had gone on this crusade for a coherent ideological or principled reason. But his post-ousting demagoguery and grandstanding about issues completely unrelated to McCarthy's job performance proved it was a personal matter."I don't think voting against Kevin McCarthy is chaos," Gaetz explained."I think $33 trillion in debt is chaos. I think that facing a $2.2 trillion annual deficit is chaos." Now, there are numerous people to blame for the impending fiscal disaster, but McCarthy is no more guilty than most.One of the least convincing claims by Gaetz's defenders is that McCarthy was punished for ignoring the base. "The base," of course, is a popular euphemism for the most vociferous populist faction of the GOP.This faction enjoys blowing things up - mostly their own party's prospects. In this case, the "base" was represented by eight Republicans and the entire Democratic Party.And among these principled eight GOPers who were fighting for the honor of the base - what The New York Times called the "far-right GOP faction" - were Reps.Nancy Mace (who said Gaetz was a "fraud" the last time he tried to knock off McCarthy) and Ken Buck (who we last heard was reportedly looking for a CNN gig). I'm going to go out on a limb and say that the future of conservatism was not the motivating factor for their votes.Most Trump-endorsed candidates didn't even participate in McCarthy's removal. Donald Trump himself tepidly supported the speaker because, as he noted, the man had said "very great things" about him. And, really, what's more important? Though, I bet McCarthy was expecting a far more energetic defense after pathetically ingratiating himself to the former president a couple of weeks ago.Even if Gaetz had excellent reasons, Republicans did not eject McCarthy.Eight Republicans can't do anything by themselves. No, 208 Democrats ousted McCarthy with the help of some petulant backbenchers nursing personal vendettas. It is a political coup for the Dems.Gaetz, who only yesterday was going on about McCarthy's "secret deal" with Democrats, had no qualms sitting on the opposition side of the House plotting to oust a speaker who holds a rickety nine-seat majority. If there was actually a brewing House rebellion, Gaetz would have been able to corral far more votes.But Gaetz wanted to "break the fever" of D.C., so he teamed up with minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, "the squad," Adam Schiff and so on. Jeffries claimed he was supporting Gaetz's efforts because Republicans have shown an "unwillingness to break from MAGA extremism in an authentic and comprehensive manner." The notion that Democrats are backing a leading MAGA loyalist because they want to temper the "extremism" of Republicans makes about as much sense as Jamaal Bowman's fire alarm story. Democrats keep pretending they yearn for a more responsible GOP and stable political environment, then keep supporting every fringe effort and candidate to undermine both.Of course, no one is owed anything.McCarthy isn't the only person available in D.C. to serve as a middling speaker of the House. And, frankly, if he'd been more talented at the job, he might have headed off this challenge more effectively. But it's doubtful anyone is going to perform better with a slender majority and the Senate and presidency in Democrats' hands.But then again, none of that matters when you're having a tantrum.

title: Julia Child's kitchen at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Julia Child's kitchen at the library

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life

 On Monday, March 3, at 6 p.m., in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, it will be my honor to interview Paula Johnson about her newest book, "Julia Child's Kitchen: The Design, Tools, Stories, and Legacy of an Iconic Space."Full disclosure: Johnson is a lifelong friend of mine. She is also a distinguished curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Among her many curatorial triumphs, it was Johnson and co-curator Rayna Green that brought Julia Child's kitchen to the museum in 2001. Almost a quarter of a century later, it remains one of that institution's most popular exhibits.
I was one of the lucky fellows who received a copy of Johnson's new book when it came out in October.
Initially, truth be told, I wasn't sure what I would think of a book about a kitchen, fool that I am. Anyone who knows Julia Child, read her books or watched her television shows, knows that a book about Julia Child's kitchen is a book about Julia Child.
It's been a long time since I've had so much fun reading a book.
And the word "fun" is apt. Again and again in the book, as people recall cooking with Child in her kitchen or a meal they shared there, the word they use to describe both their host and the place is "fun."
Which is not to say that serious labor did not take place in that kitchen.
The book makes it clear that Child and her husband Paul were both workhorses. In the early television shows, the sponsoring public television station, WGBH Boston, couldn't afford retakes or editing. Julia had to begin upon a complicated recipe, carry it through, instructing all along, and arrive at a finished product that she could take a bite out of in just 28 minutes flat. The cameras shut off at 28 minutes, and there was no going back.
To accomplish this feat of legerdemain, she and Paul would practice for hours at home before a show, choosing which elements of a recipe to demonstrate, deciding how to demonstrate those elements and carefully working out the language to use in explaining them.
The whole thing was choreographed from beginning to end and different stages of the cooking prepared in advance so that, "through the magic of TV," they could be displayed at the proper time as if just pulled from the oven.
Yet somehow, Julia always came across as relaxed and enjoying herself. And it wasn't a guise.
One of the things I found most endearing about "Julia Child's Kitchen" is the way sections on subjects such as the kitchen's organizing principles inevitably end up revealing the love Paul Child felt for his wife, the care he took in setting up that kitchen and showcasing her art. In letters to his brother, Paul sometimes referred to his wife as "Julie."
Julia called her kitchen "the soul of the house," and her nephew, Alex Prud'homme, called the table where meals were served in that kitchen "the center of the universe."
Unsurprisingly for that time and a family of their class, the Childs had a formal dining room, but Julia's preferred place to serve friends a meal was the kitchen. Julia's unpretentious attitude toward entertaining (and herself) is made clear in her explanation for the placement of that kitchen table, "I want the dining table in the middle of the room because, like a sheepdog, I need to be right there in the midst of everyone."
That statement is so characteristic of the woman we meet in Johnson's book. Julia Child never fails to charm, yet somehow she never seems to patronize or fawn.
The book itself is like a party at Julia's house. You meet fascinating people, hear terrific stories, experience a magical place, and, at the very least, get to imagine yourself enjoying extraordinary meals.
Speaking of stories, I can tell you from long experience that the author of "Julia Child's Kitchen" is a great storyteller in person as well as in her writing. And so I ask the pleasure of your company on March 3 at 6 p.m. for an evening in Julia Child's kitchen, courtesy of the Smithsonian's Paula Johnson. Trust me, you're in for a real treat.

 The Kent Cultural Alliance announces its first class of visiting artists for the SFW Residency for spring 2024.This inaugural residency session features three talented artists and educators from Alvin, Texas; Baltimore, Maryland; and Luray, Virginia. These artists will work under a collective theme of "land" as they explore agriculture, soil, family farms and more with local partners for the session — Kent County 4-H, Kent County High School Future Farmers of America, and Harborview Farms.
This social practice residency has its foundation in community engagement and seeks to create broader participation around issues important to the people who call this county home.
THE ARTISTS
Canadian-American Austen Camille is an artist, writer, builder and naturalist whose studio practice is built on her early years moving schools and cities and working to note the particularities of a place. Residing in Alivn, Texas, Camille seeks reciprocal relationships between the built and natural environment in her work. Camille's interdisciplinary practice incorporates painting, sculpture, installation, writing, research, performance, new technologies and localized materials. She seeks to forge connections between the arts and other disciplines through it. She received her BA in studio art at Reed College and her MFA in painting at Temple University.
Alyssa Dennis is an interdisciplinary artist, earth activist, educator and clinical herbalist from Baltimore, Maryland. Her art practice centers on conventional forms of building and the convenience that keeps us compartmentalized within a dangerously abstract relationship with nature and our own bodies. The imagery she creates explores the impact of manufactured landscapes on our internal and external ecosystems, shaping our existence with non-human life and, ultimately, ourselves. Dennis's work combines drawing, sculptural installation and the social/environmental practice of herbalism. In her multidisciplinary practice, she questions who the players are and what are the means for reclaiming non-human kinships as a necessary form of embodiment for the reversal of cultural and climate upheaval.
With a focus on printmaking, sculpture, storytelling and community, Dennis McNett is a multifaceted maker. Hailing from Luray, Virginia, he is known for his larger-than-life woodcut print-covered puppets and masks that are used to lead narrative ceremonies and public processions. McNett has had more than 30 visiting artist and lecturer appointments across the U.S. and abroad. He holds a BFA from Old Dominion University and an MFA from Pratt Institute, where he taught from 2004-2013. His works have been featured internationally at the Victoria and Albert Museum, the MOHS exhibit, the Museum of Print History and more.

title: Trappe Council introduces ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe Council introduces ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees

 May 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 381
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Council introduced an ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees.The introduction of Ordinance 3-2024 would amend section 14 of the Trappe Town Code to increase the water and sewer monthly fees for usage.
The monthly water usage rate is $4.70 per 1,000 gallons, and it's being proposed that it go to $6.20 per 1,000. The monthly sewer usage rate is currently $10.98 per 1,000, and it is proposed that it go to $11.48 per 1,000.
The base fees would not be increased, but the usage fees would be. Commissioner Brian Schmidt, council president, said that though the council does not like to increase fees, the town is in "desperate" need of it.
Schmidt said Trappe currently has three pumping stations that need repair, which would cost roughly $3 million. He also added that Trappe has a $13 million wastewater treatment plant that also needs repairs.
"While we hate to increase rates, the financial stability of the town is kind of in need of it," Schmidt said.
Additionally, the council approved introducing Ordinance 2-2024, adopting the FY2025 budget. This budget established a property tax rate of 33 cents per $100 of assessed real property value and 75 cents per $100 on commercial or business, personal property or public utility.
It also established an annual fee of $182 per residential household for trash collection service and adopted an enterprise budget for the town's water and sewer operations.
Erin Braband, Trappe administrator, pointed out that the tax rate for assessed real property and business personal property is not increasing, and the trash rate is not increasing.
Finally, the council approved the transfer of wastewater allocation from six lots in the Lakeside at Trappe development to the community pool for Lakeside residents.
Lakeside has purchased 120 units and issued 114 permits for homes to be built. The remaining six lots will go toward the community pool.
"We're transferring the sewer allocation from those six lots to the community center lots, so there's sewer allocation for the restrooms in the community center," Attorney Ryan Showalter said. "And this agreement basically says we're not going to build houses on those lots for occupancy, we're not gonna open anything for occupancy until the new treatment plant is open."
The council unanimously approved the agreement for wastewater allocation and development restrictions.

title: Voter turnout: 13M more nonvoters than Trump backers; Harris got 10% fewer votes than Biden
author: Mike Sunnucks
content:
Voter turnout: 13M more nonvoters than Trump backers; Harris got 10% fewer votes than Biden

 November 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks | Section: News 
 
 1205
 Words 

 Read News Document

 More than 89 million voting eligible Americans didn't vote in the 2024 elections, according to the latest tallies collected by the University of Florida's Election Lab.That accounts for more than 36.4% of the U.S. total electorate of 244.7 million people (voters and nonvoters).
There are still some votes being counted in California and Arizona.
But as it stands as of Thursday, Nov. 14, there were 13.2 million more nonvoters than supporters of now President-elect Donald Trump in the 2024 White House race.
Trump — who defeated Vice President Kamala Harris — has received close to 75.9 million votes, according to tallies Thursday from The Associated Press.
That accounts for just over 50% of the popular vote. But if nonvoters are included Trump got 31% of the electorate (voting and nonvoting).
Harris, the sitting U.S. vice president, has received close to 72.9 million votes, as of Thursday's counts.
That is more than 16.2 million fewer votes than the number of non-voters. As it stands, Harris got 29.7% of the total U.S. electorate.
Harris was installed at the top of the ticket after President Joe Biden was pressured by Democratic Party leaders and donors to quit the race in late July over concerns about his advanced age. There were some polls showing U.S. voters viewing that installation as 'undemocratic.'
Biden got close to 81.3 million in 2020 when he defeated Trump. That is more than 8.3 million more votes than Harris got in 2024. There were also more than 4.1 million fewer voters overall in 2024 compared to 2020.
Ani Ruhil, associate dean for research and planning and professor at Ohio University's Voinovich School of Leadership and Public Service, said ongoing vote counts could impact final turnout figures.
But Ruhil sees lower turnout as a key trend line in the 2024 race that saw Trump return to the White House.
"Only seven states exceeded their 2020 turnout rate — Georgia, Michigan, North Dakota, Vermont and Wisconsin," Ruhil said. "Washington, D.C., had an especially poor showing compared to 2020. So did Oregon, New Jersey, Maryland, Alaska, Illinois, and Utah."
The number of voters casting ballots in 2024 was down 11.6% in New Jersey, 11.2% in Illinois, 8.9% in Oregon and 4.6% in Washington state compared to 2020.
Nationally, turnout stands at 63.6%, according to the University of Florida. Ruhil said turnout in 2020 — which totaled 66.6% nationally — was a political aberration.
The Biden-Trump 2020 race occurred in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw more than 1.1 million deaths in the U.S., millions of workers facing job cuts and reduced hours, mask mandates and closures of schools, business and social events.
"Turnout was fanned by fear and anger," he said.
"In comes President Biden, with the singular charge of steering the country through the pandemic, and of making sure the economy did not fall to pieces. But by 2023, as we came out of the pandemic, inflation had taken its toll. Now was not the fear of a virus, but rather of gaping holes in the pocketbook. But there was no comforting plan being put forth by the White House," Ruhil continued.
He sees some voter fatigue with continued efforts by federal and state prosecutors to go after Trump.
Seventy percent of voters said the U.S. is headed in the wrong direction, with two-thirds stressed about inflation and the economy. Prices are up more than 20% since the pandemic and from when Biden and Harris took office in 2021, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Voters worried about the economy and high prices favored Trump in the 2024 race, according to exit polls.
The war in Gaza between Israel and Hamas after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks also challenged Harris.
Anti-war voters (including Muslims and Arab Americans) are upset with U.S. military support for Israel. In the other corner, supporters of Israel (including more conservative Jewish voters) didn't trust Harris to continue U.S. support for Israel . The U.S. has allocated $17.9 billion war aid to Israel since Hamas's 2023 attacks, according to Brown University.
Harris got just over 80,000 fewer votes in Michigan, where the Israel-Hamas war is an issue for Arab-American and Muslim voters, than Biden 2020.
She lost to Trump by just over 80,600 votes in Michigan.
Ruhil said the enthusiasm was let out of the turnout balloon for many Democratic voters.
"The late switch, fevered fundraising, and a hastily assembled campaign did nothing to instill confidence," he said, stressing the lack of a convincing economic message from Harris.
Harris' campaign raised more than $1 billion and had another $649 million in backing from outside groups, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. Trump raised $381.5 million and was aided by $711 million in outside spending, according to CRP.
Harris' campaign focused heavily on support for abortion rights, casting Trump as a fascist threat to democracy and procuring celebrity endorsements including Oprah Winfrey, Jennifer Lopez, Beyonce, Willie Nelson and Bruce Springsteen.
The effort fell short with Harris underperforming Biden by 8.4 million votes (or 10.3%) nationally. She saw lower turnout or flat support levels in key Electoral College battlegrounds that Trump won.
Harris got 6.6% fewer votes than Biden in Arizona.
There was also the dynamic of Trump carrying states such as Montana, Missouri, Arizona and Florida, where there were abortion rights measures also on the ballot.
Those measures all passed and in Florida an abortion rights measure got 57% of the vote (failing to meet the state's 60% threshold). Trump got 56% of the vote.
In Montana, Trump carried the state with 58%. An abortion rights measure got the same percentage.
Trump favors allowing states to decide the abortion issue versus Harris, who backs nationally enshrining abortion rights.
Abortion rights groups were among the top backers of Harris.
"This result is devastating. There has been no greater champion for reproductive freedom than Vice President Kamala Harris," said Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, a leading abortion rights advocacy group.
"We know the American people are with us, and they showed us that when they passed ballot measures and elected candidates in key states to protect their rights, said Timmaraju, who worries about Trump and the GOP in charge of the White House and Congress.
Harris and Democrats had hoped for a wave of women voters supporting abortion rights in the race against Trump.
But exit polls showed Trump carrying a majority of white women who voted, and voters were more evenly split on which presidential candidate they trusted on the abortion issue than in pre-election polls.
Abortion rights opponents argue Harris' focus on expansive abortion rights turned off some voters.
"Kamala Harris and Tim Walz support abortion anytime, anywhere, and under any circumstances. Supported by the abortion industry and its allies, Harris and Walz campaigned with fanatical fervor on abortion — and the voters rejected them," said Carol Tobias, president of National Right to Life.
Trump carried 58% of the Catholic vote versus 40% for Harris, according to NBC News exit polls. In 2020, Biden and Trump were evenly split with Catholics (49% to 50%), according to the Associated Press.
Trump won 63% of the votes from white working class women, made inroads with Hispanics (especially Hispanic men) and edged Harris with working class households, according to NBC News exit polls.
According to the University of Florida, there were 15.5 million fewer early votes in 2024 compared to 2020 (85.9 million versus 101.45 million).
That's a 15% drop.

 LANHAM - Larry Lee O'Ferrall passed away on December 5, 2023 at the age of 84 with his family by his side. He was born near East New Market in 1939, to the late Margaret and William O'Ferrall. Larry had three brothers Franklin, William, and Daniel O'Ferrall. He attended North Dorchester High School and graduated in 1957.Larry married Helen Hurlock on August 7, 1960 in Hurlock, MD. They moved to the suburbs of Washington, DC and in 1966, they had a son, Larry Allen O'Ferrall. Larry Lee has two grandchildren, Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall.
Larry worked in the computer field for the Central Intelligence Agency from 1960 to 2005. After retiring he briefly worked for the US Army as a contractor.
Larry was an avid sports fan who played baseball and football in High School as well as softball and football with the CIA. For over a decade he played softball on the same team with his son.
He was an avid reader and interested in history.
He enjoyed crabbing and fishing in the rivers on the Eastern Shore as a youth. He was a devoted family man and a proud grandparent. He was always in attendance at his grandchildren's events and games.
Besides his wife Helen, Larry is survived by Larry Allen O'Ferrall, his daughter-in-law Elizabeth O'Ferrall, his grandchildren Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall, his sister-in-law Barbara O'Ferrall and several nieces and nephews. He is preceded in death by his parents and brothers.
A viewing and funeral service will be held at the Zeller Funeral Home in East New Market, MD on Sunday, December 17th. The viewing will be at 1 pm and service at 2 pm. The burial will follow immediately at the Unity Washington Cemetery in Hurlock.

Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance

 EASTON — Nearly two months since opening a public hearing on the topic, the Easton Town Council has passed an ordinance revising the Town Code to regulate zoning for cannabis-related uses.At its meeting Monday, the council voted to pass Ordinance 809 with amendments.
The amended ordinance permits the use of dispensaries through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district and the general commercial district. It also permits, through special exception, cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments are prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the ordinance.
The passing of the ordinance comes about nine months after the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses took effect. In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits, which expires May 9.
"If we don't vote today, we must at the next meeting in order to be handled before our moratorium expires," Council President Frank Gunsallus said at the meeting Monday.
The council waited to vote on the topic while the General Assembly discussed the topic in Annapolis. At the council meeting April 1, Easton Town Planner Lynn Thomas said the Maryland Senate had passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates. He said said that, considering the General Assembly would be adjourning, the town should have the information it needs to vote at April 15's Town Council meeting.
At the meeting Monday, Easton Director of Planning and Zoning Miguel Salinas said that House Bill 805, which deals with cannabis restrictions, had gone through the Senate and House of Delegates and is now awaiting Gov. Wes Moore's signature.
Salinas listed the amendments to Easton's ordinance, including a separation requirement of a half mile between dispensaries. Salinas said that is in House Bill 805.
Salinas said other amendments to the ordinance include the addition of parking standards for dispensaries and the addition of a requirement that a professional engineer or equivalent qualified professional certify that that the proposed odor measures established effectively eliminate outdoor odors.
Before voting on the ordinance, Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello asked that they change the ordinance to permit cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district through special exception, rather than just permitting it.
"There's one industrial area in particular that is off of Dover Road that backs right up to an entire neighborhood," Abbatiello said. "I'm sure that those individuals would at least like the opportunity to share their concerns or joy that a growing facility is going in that area."
Abbatiello said this change would not prohibit growing and processing facilities from the industrial zoning district, it would just give residents "an extra opportunity" to voice their thoughts.
Gunsallus made a motion at the meeting to approve the ordinance with the amendments from the town and the amendment requested by Abbatiello, which passed.
At the end of the meeting, Abbatiello thanked Thomas, Salinas and Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh for their work on the ordinance.
"This has been a long process," he said. "It's been a difficult process. And I really do appreciate all their effort to give us the best information so that we can make a decision."

title: Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership
author: LENA GILL
content:
Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership

 June 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LENA GILL | Section: Columns 
 
 713
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The U.S. higher educational system may in future years lose $38 billion a year. This is the estimated annual contribution by foreign students. In the school year 2023-2024 it was estimated that 1.1 million foreign students were studying at universities across the U.S., and they generally pay full fare or do work/study. They supported about 378,000 academic jobs.Now we risk driving them away.
On April 19, CNN reported that thousands of international students across the country were informed by email that their student visas were revoked. Six days later the Trump administration decided to restore 1,400 student visas. How many students did not have their visas restored is unknown. We do know that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a list of about 300 students that he planned to expel. The National Immigration Project is challenging the visa cancellations in court.
Apart from the money that these foreign students bring in, why would we care? Because foreign students began many of the successful startups in Silicon Valley. We care because much research in science done at our universities has brought the U.S. to a revered leadership position in the world in medical science research.
With a stroke of the president's pen this may all disappear. The best brains in the world will not want to come here anymore. Research in advanced cancer treatments, drugs to treat Alzheimer, sudden crib deaths as well as CRISPRs use in treating genetic blood disorders by cutting out a person's faulty DNA will not continue without federal support. The U.S. inventors of CRISPR won the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 2020. We will be taking a giant step backward in the sciences.
In the 20th century up to World War II, Germany won about 30% of the Nobel Prizes in science. The second runner-up was Great Britain with 20% of the Nobel Prizes in science. The U.S. was way down the list with only 6% of the Nobel Prizes in science.
What turned the tide was Adolf Hitler who drove many of the best German scientists, artists and architects (some of them Jewish) to U.S. universities in the 1930s, where they were welcomed. The second German brain drain happened immediately after the war when U.S. intelligence invited physicists like Wernher von Braun (inventor of the German rockets) to the U.S. to work for the space program. The U.S. emerged from the war economically, technologically and militarily better than the rest of the world.
What really propelled the U.S. into today's leadership position was the futuristic vision of what could come, if the U.S. government funded basic research at universities small and large around the country with a promise to keep the government's hands off. The academic freedom and competition created by this decision attracted the best brains from around the world.
Since 2000, the U.S. has won 72 Nobel Prizes in science, of which about 30% were won by immigrants. Great Britain won 16, Germany 7, France 5, Japan 9, Israel 5. Canada, Australia.and Norway won three each.
This rosy picture will change fast if the Trump administration continues to threaten leading universities with withdrawal of funds and academic freedom. Harvard University, which so far has not backed down, was threatened with cancellation of its not-for-profit designation. $2 billion in research grants were withdrawn by the administration. Foreign students' and researchers' visas are being revoked. 27% of the students are from abroad. Attacking an elite university may appeal to the MAGA base, but it is still difficult to understand why President Trump wants to destroy the foremost academic institution in the US!
The Trump administration also is threatening withdrawal of funds from our other world-renowned science research facilities, the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. A science publication asked its readers if they were affected by government harassment and withdrawal of funds. If so, were they considering moving their research elsewhere? 75% of the 1,600 who responded said they were considering it.
With a stroke of the president's pen, we have lost 75 years of leadership in the sciences.
California, Texas, Illinois, Massachusetts and New York will see the most economic impact. Maryland also will suffer, as we are home to Johns Hopkins Hospital, the site of original cancer research and treatment, and the University of Maryland Medical Center with its world-renowned Shock Trauma Center.

title: Candy hearts and other Valentine's treats
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Candy hearts and other Valentine's treats

 February 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The big day is here, and the traditions of flowers and chocolates still holds their spots as number one favorites for all ages.My favorite Valentine's Day memories are of the elementary school parties — the cute cards and little candy hearts. The girls would gather and compare the message candies from the boys.
What fun that was. Then came high school, and the stakes were higher. The cute juvenile cards turned into single rose buds and candy.
No matter how you celebrate this special day — with or without candy — just tell that special person (or persons) "happy Valentine's Day."
HEART SHAPED PIZZA
1 pound store-bought pizza dough, 1 tbsp olive oil (plus more for brushing), 16 slices pepperoni, All-purpose flour (for dusting), 1/2 cup prepared pizza sauce, 1 cup shredded low-moisture mozzarella. Put the pizza dough in a medium bowl and coat well with the olive oil. Cover with plastic wrap and allow to sit at room temperature for 1 hour. Meanwhile, put a large inverted baking sheet on the lowest oven rack and preheat the oven to 500 degrees. Fold a pepperoni slice in half and use a pair of kitchen shears to trim the edges into the shape of half of a heart. When you unfold the pepperoni slice, it will be a whole heart. Repeat this process with the remaining pepperoni, then set aside.
Divide the pizza dough into 2 balls. On a lightly floured surface, stretch 1 ball of dough into a 10-inch round. Transfer the dough to a piece of parchment paper, then slide the parchment and dough onto a second inverted baking sheet. Use a pair of kitchen shears or a paring knife to cut the pizza dough into the shape of a large heart, discarding the dough scraps. Spread half of the sauce on the dough in a thin layer and scatter half of the mozzarella on top. Top with half of the pepperoni slices. Use a pastry brush to brush the exposed edges of the dough with olive oil. Carefully slide the parchment onto the preheated baking sheet and bake until the crust is golden brown and the cheese is bubbling, 6 to 8 minutes. Let cool for 1 to 2 minutes before slicing. Repeat to make a second pizza.
SURF AND TURF
1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley, 2 tbsps chopped fresh chives, 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, Kosher salt and freshly ground pepper, 6 jumbo shrimp (peeled and deveined, tails intact), 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, juice of 1/2 lemon, 2 tsps chopped fresh thyme (plus 2 to 3 sprigs), freshly ground pepper, 6 slices pancetta (about 2 ounces), 1 10-ounce piece beef tenderloin (trimmed), sea salt, 8 asparagus spears, 1 tbsp unsalted butter. Pulse the parsley, chives and olive oil in a mini food processor until smooth. Thin with water, if necessary, and add 1/4 tsp each salt and pepper. Transfer to a small bowl, cover and set aside. (This can be done up to 2 hours ahead.)
Toss the shrimp, olive oil, lemon juice, chopped thyme and pepper to taste in a bowl. Wrap each shrimp with a piece of pancetta. Preheat the broiler. Arrange the shrimp on a foil-lined broiler pan. Season the beef with sea salt and pepper, press the thyme sprigs into the meat and set aside. Snap off the tough ends of the asparagus. Put the asparagus in a microwave-safe dish with 1/4 cup water and a pinch of sea salt. Heat a medium ovenproof skillet over high heat and add the butter. When the foam subsides, sear the beef until golden brown, about 3 minutes per side. Using tongs, hold the meat and brown the sides. Transfer the skillet to the broiler and cook until a thermometer inserted into the beef registers 125 degrees for medium rare, about 4 more minutes. Transfer to a cutting board to rest while you cook the shrimp. Broil the shrimp until the pancetta is crisp, about 2 minutes per side. Meanwhile, microwave the asparagus until tender, about 2 minutes. Slice the beef into 4 pieces. Serve with the shrimp, herb oil and asparagus.
CLASSIC SPAGHETTI AND MEATBALLS
1 pound spaghetti, 1 pound ground beef, 1/3 cup breadcrumbs, 1/4 cup finely chopped parsley, 1/4 cup freshly grated parmesan (plus more for serving), 1 large egg, 2 garlic cloves (minced), Kosher salt, 1/2 tsp. red pepper flakes, 2 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1/2 cup onion (finely chopped), 1 (28-oz.) can crushed tomatoes, 1 bay leaf, freshly ground black pepper.
In a large pot of salted boiling water, cook pasta until al dente. Drain. In a large bowl, combine beef with breadcrumbs, parsley, parmesan, egg, garlic, 1 tsp salt and red pepper flakes. Mix until just combined, then form into 16 balls. In a large pot over medium heat, heat oil. Add meatballs and cook, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 10 minutes. Transfer meatballs to a plate. Add onion to pot and cook until soft, 5 minutes. Add crushed tomatoes and bay leaf. Season with salt and pepper and bring to a simmer. Return meatballs to pot and cover. Simmer until the sauce has thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Serve pasta with a healthy scoop of meatballs and sauce.
VALENTINES DAY SUGAR COOKIES
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour (plus more for dusting), 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1 1/2 sticks unsalted butter (at room temperature), 3/4 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp pure vanilla extract, 1 large egg. For Icing: 3 cups confectioners' sugar, 1/4 cup plus 2 tbsps milk, 1 1/2 tsps pure vanilla extract, red gel food coloring, pink gel food coloring, sprinkles (optional). Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper.
For the cookies: Combine the flour, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl and set aside. In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, beat the butter, sugar and vanilla on medium-high speed until light and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Add the egg and mix until fully incorporated, about 1 minute. Reduce the speed to low, add the flour mixture and mix until well combined, scraping down sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula as needed, about 2 minutes.
Divide the dough into 2 equal pieces. Working with 1 piece at a time, roll the dough on a lightly floured piece of parchment paper until it's about 1/8-inch thick. Using heart-shaped cookie cutters, cut the dough and place the cookies on the prepared baking sheets about 1 inch apart (a small off-set spatula is really helpful when transferring the cookies). After both pieces of dough have been rolled out and cut, combine the dough scraps and re-roll and cut to utilize as much of the dough as possible. Bake until the cookies are just barely golden around the edges, rotating halfway through, 12 to 14 minutes. Transfer the cookies to wire racks to cool completely.
For the icing: Whisk the confectioners' sugar, milk and vanilla in a medium bowl until smooth. The consistency should be similar to that of slightly thinned yogurt and should coat the back of a spoon. Adjust with additional confectioners' sugar or milk, if needed. Place 2 tbsps of icing into each of 2 small bowls. Add 4 drops of red gel food coloring to one bowl and 2 drops of pink gel food coloring to the other and stir until fully incorporated. Using a small spoon, drizzle a small amount of each color over the white icing and then repeatedly drag a toothpick through the icing until you create a marbled effect.
Working with one cooled cookie at a time, carefully dip it face-side down into the icing and allow any excess to drip off before placing the cooking back on the cooling rack. Add additional red and pink icing to the bigger bowl of icing as needed to maintain the marbling effect.
HOMEMADE CANDY HEARTS
1 1/4-ounce packet unflavored gelatin powder, 1 tbsp light corn syrup, 1/2 tsp vanilla extract, 1/8 tsp salt, 2 1-pound boxes confectioners' sugar (plus more for kneading), assorted food coloring (for tinting), assorted extracts (such as peppermint, strawberry or almond) for flavoring, cooking spray. Whisk the gelatin, corn syrup, vanilla, salt and 1/2 cup boiling water in a stand mixer bowl until the gelatin dissolves. Using the paddle attachment, beat in the confectioners' sugar on medium-low speed, 1 cup at a time, to make a stiff, sticky dough.
Transfer the dough to a clean surface and knead, adding more confectioners' sugar as needed (up to 1 cup), until the dough is smooth, pliable and slightly tacky, about 5 minutes. Divide the dough into 4 pieces. Flatten 1 piece into a disk. (Cover the rest with plastic wrap.) Add a few drops each of food coloring and extract to the center of the dough; fold in the sides and pinch closed, then knead until the color is distributed.
Lightly coat a large piece of parchment paper with cooking spray. Roll out the colored dough on the parchment until 1/8 to 1/4 inch thick. Cut into hearts using 1-inch cookie cutters; transfer to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Repeat with the remaining dough, using different colors and extracts. Let the hearts sit at room temperature, uncovered, until dry and hard, about 24 hours, flipping them halfway through. Write messages on the hearts using food decorating pens. Store in an airtight container for up to 1 week.

title: Harris speaks to Dorchester Chamber after rally calling for town hall
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Harris speaks to Dorchester Chamber after rally calling for town hall

 March 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 748
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Hours after a rally was held questioning Rep. Andy Harris' (R-Md. 1st) loyalty to his constituents, Harris told Dorchester Chamber of Commerce members inside the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina that his office is here to help them."We can make your business run easier," he said during his keynote speech for the chamber's 79th annual business meeting and dinner. "We can work through the bureaucracy. Please get in touch with my office. We're more than happy to help you."
Earlier that evening, protesters lined the sidewalks of U.S. Route 50 outside the Hyatt, calling on Harris to hold a town hall and questioning whether Harris' allegiance is to his constituents or to Elon Musk and the Trump administration. The rally was organized by Cambridge Indivisible, a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Speaking to members of the media after the chamber dinner, Harris said he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents.
"They're brought in by buses," he said. "I don't know where those buses come from. And we know that the national Indivisibles are involved. So we believe that a lot of those people aren't even constituents."
Harris said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's going on" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there. He said he would not name who told him that.
"This is astroturf," he said. "This is not grassroots."
Cambridge Indivisible Founder and Chair Michelle Fowle said many of those at the rally were her neighbors who live in Cambridge.
"He's just a liar," she said about Harris.
Harris said he will be holding a virtual town hall on March 25 so he can communicate with constituents from all over his district.
"If these protesters want to call in, if they want to get on my town hall, I will answer that question on my town hall," he said. "But I'm not going to hold a town hall for 100 people when I could hold a town hall and reach out to 5,000 people who don't have to leave their homes, get bused in by some entity paying for that bus."
Harris said he is "laser focused" on working for his constituents and advancing the Trump administration's agenda.
"Who also won the district with high numbers," he said about President Donald Trump (R) getting elected in November.
In Dorchester County, Trump won 55.99% of the vote, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections.
During the rally before the chamber dinner, protesters brought up concerns with recent mass firings of federal workers. Suzanne Sullivan said she has concerns about what the firings will do for the local economy. Sullivan, who lives in Dorchester County, is the wife of environmental scientist Jake Shaner, who was recently fired from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Harris told media after the dinner that most companies layoff employees every three to five years. He said that with federal tax cuts, the federal government will grow the economy so there are "plenty of jobs for every American."
"Look, do I feel for everybody who's laid off?" he asked. "Absolutely. Private industry, public government. It's a personal family setback. That's exactly why we have unemployment insurance and we have the social net until these individuals find another job."
HARRIS' KEYNOTE SPEECH
During his keynote speech, Harris touched on a number of issues relevant to Dorchester County and the Eastern Shore. He spoke about the importance of the agriculture industry, low-cost energy and the H-2B visa program.
Harris also brought up the need for blue catfish processing centers to help reduce the population of the invasive species in the Chesapeake Bay. He said federal funding will be available to entrepreneurs who want to build processing plants so the catfish can be considered a commercially viable seafood product.
Harris said two things the county should focus on are addressing drug and alcohol addiction and making sure every child is reading on grade level.
"And we can certainly provide help from the federal government," he said. "But I'll tell you, some of the best solutions are at the local level."
Harris, who lives in Cambridge, said it is a pleasure to represent the people of the Eastern Shore. He said he lives a "blessed life" where he can be at Mar-a-Lago one night and eating at Cindy's Kitchen in Cambridge the next morning.
"It's like the best of both worlds," he said. "And to be honest with you, I like Cindy's better. But don't tell the president that."

title: Towns need to balance pride in past with future
author: BRANDON WRIGHT
content:
Towns need to balance pride in past with future

 May 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BRANDON WRIGHT | Section: Columns 
 
 805
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently, I listened to a webinar about the challenges of planning, land use and economic development in rural areas. Communities frequently struggle to grow and still maintain their character. Balancing economic growth with the community's heritage is among the most significant challenges for elected officials because the two are often intertwined.An industry of consultants has grown up to help communities meet these challenges. Like the consultants, I believe a balance can be reached.
Maybe I am too much of an optimist, but I think opposing groups can find common ground if they are honest and transparent. I served as chief of staff in the Maryland Department of Planning nearly 10 years ago. I met with town council members, county commissioners and local business leaders, all vested in making their communities strong and vibrant. My confidence comes from listening to their hopes, dreams and goals for their communities.
I met with the consultants, too. Everyone wanted the same for the community — the absolute best.
Compromises that are in the best interests of all the various constituencies and stakeholders can be forged, even in rural Maryland like the Eastern Shore. There is no place like it. Its ecosystems and economies are different, even from other rural parts of the state. So much of the economy is dependent on the Chesapeake Bay and the rivers that feed into it. It is teeming with myriad species of animals on land and sea.
The motto of Federalsburg, my hometown in Caroline County, is "Pride in the Past, Faith in the Future." Unfortunately in towns like Federalsburg, more emphasis is placed on the past than the future. Local officials, sometimes pressured by citizens, have these gauzy memories of a better time and place in the community's past and yearn to get back to it.
However, in doing so, they strip decision-makers of any chance at finding the right balance between the past and future, choking off opportunities to attract large employers, employees and all the businesses that spring up to support them both.
As a young boy, I fished for bass and perch on the Marshyhope Creek, the northwest fork of the Nanticoke River. I heard the story that the DuPont Company was looking to build its new nylon factory in the area, and the Marshyhope Creek made Federalsburg an attractive site. Unfortunately, DuPont built its nylon plant on the Nanticoke River in Seaford, Delaware, less than 10 miles from Federalsburg. The plant was constructed outside the town, and Seaford quickly became a company town. The contrast between the two towns is dramatic.
Federalsburg missed out again, this time on AquaCon. An international salmon farming operation would have brought several hundred well-paying jobs, jobs with health care and all the other benefits that help smooth the rough edges of life. AquaCon would have increased revenue to the town, support for existing small businesses and all the different services that make a small town tick.
Town officials, under pressure from citizens, said no to this opportunity. Rather than work with the company to better understand the project and address concerns, the town leaders said no and now another community will benefit from these jobs and the economic development that comes with it.
According to state data, Caroline County is among the most economically depressed counties in Maryland. We can't lay all the blame at the feet of elected leaders for that. I know many of them, and each one cares deeply for the communities they serve; otherwise, they wouldn't do it. The blame, however, should be shared with the voters that elected them and the voters who pushed the elected leaders to say no to investments in the towns that would spur economic growth over fears of the unknown and fears of something different, a break from the past.
Because the citizens share the blame, they are responsible for turning their communities around.
Our rural communities are blessed with resources that other towns and cities envy. We have kind, friendly people who care for each other. We have the greatest renewable resource of all — an unending stream of smart and talented young men and women graduating from our high schools and colleges, prepared to make the world a better place. Let's do everything we can to keep them here.
Let our legacy be that we found that balance that everyone strives for and leave the next generation and the generations that follow a community poised for growth, good jobs and continued access to outstanding education. Let's be sure we live up to the motto, "Pride in the Past, Faith in the Future."
Brandon Wright grew up in Federalsburg and graduated from Colonel Richardson High School in 1997 and Salisbury University in 2001. He was the chief of staff at the Maryland Department of Planning from 2015 to 2017. He now lives in Annapolis, but his family still resides just outside of Federalsburg.

title: Always plenty to be thankful for in Maryland
author: Staff Writer
content:
Always plenty to be thankful for in Maryland

 November 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It should be easy for most of us to be thankful in Maryland. Thanksgiving has just about arrived, that special day for reflection, for sharing our gratitude and for enjoying a splendidly large meal with those we love.We've mostly been spared the political rancor that marked much of the election season nationwide. The local campaigning leading up to filling out our ballots earlier this fall was mostly crisp and clean.
So as we prepare ourselves for the Thanksgiving holiday, let's hope that peace and civility will prevail, at least for a day. Let's hope that when extended families convene for the old familiar feast, debate won't rage between red and blue, but about whether dark meat is more delicious than white meat as the turkey is carved.
Thanksgiving is a legacy of early colonial America, when European settlers thanked God for the harvest that allowed people to survive under difficult conditions. These days, of course, only a dwindling portion of our population here still has lives so closely tied to the harvest. Most of us take comfortable shelter and an adequate food supply for granted every day.
Did you know that we have a president, a secretary of state and the author of "Mary Had A Little Lamb" to thank for Thanksgiving becoming a fully recognized holiday in the United States?
Editor and writer Sarah Josepha Hale launched her campaign in 1827 to see the annual Thanksgiving tradition dating back a couple hundred years become an official holiday. She started with President John Quincy Adams — son of Founding Father John Adams — and finally found success many years later with President Abraham Lincoln in 1863. Secretary of State William Seward penned Lincoln's proclamation, which came in "the midst of a civil war of unequalled magnitude and severity."
"I do, therefore, invite my fellow-citizens in every part of the United States, and also those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands, to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next as a Day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the heavens," Lincoln's proclamation reads.
Well, 2024 has certainly been a year, but we still have so much to be thankful for, each and everyone of us.
In a way, we're all accidents of birth, and ongoing accidents of geography. We could be anywhere else in the world — and plenty of those places have more than enough misery to go around. Gratitude for our peace, safety and security here at home would be in order.
We should also be thankful for the people in our community who will be required to postpone their feasts to help others in need. We can take comfort in knowing that police and hospital staff will be on the job, and volunteer firefighters and other first responders could be pressed into service at any time if there's an emergency.
Then there are those thoughtful souls who make sure that anyone who wants to come out can enjoy an absolutely free hot Thanksgiving family-style meal and fellowship. Food banks, soup kitchens and churches around the region help make sure that happens.
For sure, this holiday season that officially kicks off next week and runs all the way through New Year's Day can stretch time, money and sometimes patience particularly thin. But let's face it, most of us have plenty for which to be thankful. And we should have little reason not to feel blessed and grateful on Thanksgiving and every day.
Our community is strong. And through the works large and small of all our friends and neighbors, we will only continue to get stronger. And for that, too, we offer our thanks.
Even in our nation's darkest times, Lincoln and Seward found much to be celebrated: "The year that is drawing toward its close has been filled with the blessings of fruitful fields and healthful skies. To these bounties, which are so constantly enjoyed that we are prone to forget the source from which they come, others have been added, which are of so extraordinary a nature that they cannot fail to penetrate and even soften the heart which is habitually insensible to the ever-watchful providence of Almighty God."
We can all take their words to heart as we head into the holiday season. We can look to the good. We can focus on the positive. We can find our way forward with thankfulness and love in our hearts.
We wish you all a happy Thanksgiving.
