title: Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1030
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Police Accountability Board shared its second annual report with the County Commissioners at their Feb. 6 meeting.The bottom line: Of the thousands of contacts people had with county and town law enforcement officers, a handful of complaints were made, and a fraction of those resulted in disciplinary action.
Presenting the report were Police Accountability Board Chairman John Bartlett and Board Administrator Kimberly Raeder.
Bartlett said he wanted to make one "very important" point: The Caroline County Sheriff's Office had over 26,000 calls for service in 2023, which generated only six complaints, he said.
"Five of those six were exonerated, meaning unfounded, and one was a very minor infraction, which led to a written reprimand," he said. "I think that speaks volumes with law enforcement here in Caroline County."
A state mandate
Raeder explained the purpose and scope of the three police oversight boards mandated by the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021, which became effective July 1, 2022.
The role of the county's Police Accountability Board "is to receive police complaints, recommend policy changes and identify any trends," Raeder said.
"The second board is the five-member Administrative Charging Committee, and their role is to look over and review completed complaint investigations and recommend discipline," she said. If the Charging Committee decides to administratively charge, they use the statewide police disciplinary matrix to "decide what kind of discipline would be necessary based on the complaint."
The five members of the Charging Committee were appointed and trained in April 2023 at the Fretterd Center by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission.
The third board is the Trial Board comprised of retired Maryland Circuit Court Judge Owen Wise, a citizen and a police officer of the same rank, Raeder said. No complaints have been referred to this board.
"I'm proud to say that Caroline County is leading the way for other counties on the Eastern Shore who have reached out to us regarding using Judge Wise, if they need a judge for a trial board," she said.
Few complaints filed
Among the county's municipalities, 15 complaints were filed, including a pending complaint related to an April 7, 2023, incident in Denton that prompted millions of views on YouTube, Bartlett said.
A video of the incident shows Christopher Morgan threatening the residents and breaking the window of the storm door of a home while two Denton Police officers stand on the sidewalk watching.
The way the officers handled the call for service prompted Denton Police Chief George Bacorn to request the Talbot County Sheriff's Office to investigate the handling of the incident. Their findings were turned over to the Administrative Charging Committee.
There were no complaints from Ridgely or Greensboro. One was brought to the Police Accountability Board from Federalsburg, which was exonerated, Bartlett said.
The report breaks down the 15 complaints by percentages; numerically, four complaints are pending investigation, three were administratively charged, two were withdrawn by the complainant, four were exonerated and two were "not in the purview of the ACC (Administrative Charging Committee)."
The Accountability Board identified trends in the disciplinary process and didn't "recommend any changes at this time."
"A common identified trend, however, has been the lack of activation of body cameras when officers interact with the public," the report stated. "The ACC discovered this trend when reviewing completed complaint investigations which had no body camera footage for the ACC to review. The Board advised the municipal Police Departments and the Sheriff's Office to remind Officers to adhere to department policy and activate their cameras when encountering the public. The policy protects both the Officer and the Citizen if a complaint were to arise from the interaction."
Cost to the county
Bartlett thanked the commissioners for their "financial support of the committee for legal decisions when needed."
The boards' complying with the state mandates has incurred expenses for the county, although some have been covered by the Police Accountability, Community, and Transparency Grant program.
Of the $105,272 in grant funds received, the Accountability Board has spent $49,545, which includes the purchase of IAPro software for filing complaints, annual computer licensing for all board members, and pay for the Board's administrator.
The Police Accountability Board is asking the state to continue offering these grants, as well as other police-oriented grant programs for local police departments to be able to purchase "the required technology, resources, and tools to comply with the law," including software and a change in the vendor for body cameras, so that every law enforcement agency in the county has the same system.
Other costs included outside legal counsel, with expenses the County Commissioners agreed to fund to the tune of nearly $8,000.
Questions arose requiring legal clarification for both the Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee, and the county commissioners "agreed to bear the expense of hiring outside legal counsel" to represent both. "Legal Counsel attends each quarterly meeting and provides interpretation of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021 as needed," the report stated.
The legal expenses for the Police Accountability Board were $3,650, while those of the Administrative Charging Committee amounted to $4,300.
PAB recommendations
The Accountability Board recommends "changing ACC training from all in-person training to online meeting based or pre-recorded online training. With one member of our ACC board resigning this past July, we have firsthand knowledge of the burden imposed on the newly appointed volunteer Board member. As terms end or resignations occur, the pool of applicants will continue to shrink when advised that members must undergo uncompensated training prior to serving."
Another unanticipated result of the law has been the withdrawing of multiple complaints, which created a legal conundrum for the Accountability Board and is currently being resolved with the Office of the Attorney General.
The report also suggested amending the law by mandating only complaints of "matters of public concern," that is, "police misconduct, such as abuse of power, false arrest, police brutality, or criminal activity" be referred to the Charging Committee, thus alleviating pressure on municipal police departments. "Rude and discourteous" behavior towards a citizen would be handled at the department or agency level, as suggested by the Accountability Board.
To read the full report, which includes rosters of members of the PAB and ACC boards, visit carolinemd.org/DocumentCenter/View/8606/2023-Annual-Report-PAB?bidId=. The last page provides links to other documents and resources provided by the PAB.

title: Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Calvert County School Board member Melissa Goshorn's comment at the panel's April meeting proved to be prophetic."I recognize it's going to make a lot of people unhappy," Goshorn said just prior to requesting that Superintendent of Schools Andraé Townsel to remove "Safe Space" stickers from school buildings.
Goshorn based her request on anecdotal information she received at a National School Boards Association conference during what she described as a "bone-chilling session" presented by the Beau Biden Foundation.
The story relayed to session attendees dealt with a principal who was arrested on child sex abuse charges and may have gained children's confidence by having a "Safe Space" sticker on the office door.
The sticker is widely used as a sign that LGBTQ students will not be discriminated in that space.
"I think we need to have them removed," Goshorn said.
School maintenance staff removed the stickers and the predicted unhappiness manifested itself during the board's May 8 meeting when 19 of the 20 speakers addressed the issue during the public comment segment. While a handful of the speakers indicated support for the sticker removal, many expressed opposition.
Sheri Tardio of Prince Frederick called the issue "manufactured outrage. Safe space stickers do not promote ideology. Diversity is a fact."
"You are not hiding your biases very well," said Stacy Tayman, president of the Calvert Association for Educational Support Staff.
"Removing stickers is not a violation of First Amendment rights," said school board President Jana Post in her closing comments, adding that the April discussion "was twisted" into an LGBTQ issue.
"Real safety comes from a culture of trust," Post said.
At the conclusion of public comments, board member Paul Harrison made a motion to discuss "a flag policy" at a future meeting. That policy would likely be aimed at setting parameters for displays of flags, posters and decals in school buildings. The motion passed unanimously.
Supervisor's post
The school board unanimously approved the appointment of Marc Watson as supervisor of health, physical education and athletics. The Indiana University of Pennsylvania graduate is a familiar face in Calvert County where he has previously served as a teacher, coach and principal.
Most recently, Watson served as principal of King George High School in Virginia.
Watson told the board he was looking forward to "continuing to create this wonderful environment of learning and athletics" in Calvert County.
In recommending Watson for the appointment, Townsel said the returning administrator will provide "training and mentorship for coaches."

title: For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Representatives from For All Seasons say the problem of human trafficking in Talbot County is persisting, though they are seeing positive gains in awareness and detection.During a Talbot County Council meeting Tuesday, Lauren Weber, the nonprofit's vice president of strategy and development, provided an update to council members regarding human and labor trafficking.
"It is happening and it's happening here. That continues to be the case," Weber said. " … There's a complexity to human trafficking that it doesn't really know county boundaries."
Weber and Katie Theeke, vice president of marketing and communications, each said the organization has a special role given its wide reach. For All Seasons' presence in the five Mid-Shore counties — Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot — is critical to providing victims with essential services.
"We know that human trafficking knows no boundaries and that it affects people of different backgrounds, races, genders," Theeke said. "We have seen several cases come through our doors, and it comes from Talbot County. It comes from neighboring counties. We really aim to be the connector to get those people the help that they need."
Council Member Keasha Haythe asked if For All Seasons is seeing a decline in human trafficking numbers. Weber said it's a "double-edged sword."
"A year ago we sat in front of you and said, when we look at our rape crisis center data, a good fifth of what was coming in was having at least one indicator of human trafficking," Weber said. " … That persists."
The organization has noticed a shift in how many people are recognizing signs of human trafficking and making those reports, Weber says.
"The folks that are self-referring, we're seeing a decline," she said. "But we're seeing a real rapid incline in folks coming to us and saying, 'Hey, I know more and now I've seen something.'"
Weber said that since September, more than 120 people have taken For All Seasons' free, online anti-human trafficking course.
For All Seasons is an official regional navigator for the Mid-Shore area, Theeke said, meaning it works on task forces and serves youth and young adults that are victims of trafficking.
At the end of the discussion, council members thanked the For All Seasons representatives for their work and presented the organization with a proclamation Tuesday declaring January as National Human Trafficking Awareness Month.
"We know that even one victim is too many," council Vice President Pete Lesher said. "We appreciate all that you do both on prevention, but also to develop and take care of those who have been victims."

title: CCTC AMP students present designs - Rashad Wilson's winning design adorns dartboard cabinet project
content:
CCTC AMP students present designs - Rashad Wilson's winning design adorns dartboard cabinet project

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY - The seventh cohort of Advanced Manufacturing Program students at Caroline Career and Technology Center recently presented design ideas for their current project, a dartboard cabinet.The winning design was created by Rashad Wilson, and was inspired by the doors one might find hanging in a saloon in the Old West."Rashad's dartboard design offers a new challenge for the class and me," teacher Keith Hale said.Although the students possessed the software and the capability to machine a three-dimensional object like the steer skull and horns, they had never attempted it before. "This design is more challenging than designs created by previous classes," he said.This particular project was generated three years ago when an AMP student approached Hale with the idea of manufacturing dartboard cabinets. Hale and the class were excited to make this idea a reality.Since then, AMP cabinets with dartboard with darts included have been one of AMP's most popular products, selling out even before they were presented.Each time AMP students manufacture a product, they follow the same template.It begins with research, mood-boarding and a product pitch. With dartboards, students research the history, rules and professional leagues in the game of darts. Then each student must come up with a design for the project, followed by drafting their design and placing it on a Mood Board.This Mood Board becomes a visual they can refer to as they present their product pitch.Business partners, school officials, parents and former students are then invited to watch the students' product pitches Oct. 26.One by one, students manage the difficult task of individually pitching the details and merits of their designs to the class and guests in attendance.At the end of the presentations, everyone votes and a design is chosen.The next step in the process is called "napkin sketching," which is a sketch of the product views and dimensions.These sketches are then taken to the computer aided drafting lab, where more accurate prints are made. From those prints, numeric commands are created that will drive a computer numeric control machine, which is a robot programmed to cut pieces out of stock material.Once complete, an audience is once again assembled for student presentations of the finished products, which are also offered for sale.

author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Sail Selina II to set sail in St. Michaels for final season

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 661
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After nearly a century on the water and more than two decades guiding passengers along the Miles River, the Sail Selina II will be sailing into retirement later this year.Following its upcoming season, which begins next week, Captain Iris Robertson will be retiring. But before it departs the Bay following the end of its season in November, Sail Selina II is going out with a bang.
The boat is joining the National Park Service's Chesapeake Gateways Network, a network of places that offer opportunities for visitors to learn about and enjoy the Chesapeake Bay.
Robertson said in the last 25 years, she estimates close to 60,000 people have stepped aboard Sail Selina II. Some of those passengers, she said, might not have gotten out on the water otherwise.
"The Bay is very fragile," Robertson said. "It's at risk right now. And (for) folks that live in Pennsylvania, (it's) out of sight, out of mind. But they're on the watershed. And Selina's just been a wonderful way for people to connect to something that they participate in even though it's not necessarily in their backyard."
On April 24, there will be a ribbon cutting ceremony at the Harbour Inn Marina in St. Michaels to welcome Sail Selina II into the Chesapeake Gateways Network for its final season. The event will include remarks from National Park Service Chesapeake Gateways Superintendent Wendy O'Sullivan.
GENERATIONS ON THE WATERAlthough Robertson, who lives in Royal Oak, has been the captain of Sail Selina II for 25 years, her history with the boat stretches back to before she was born.
In 1926, Robertson's grandfather had the boat commissioned. Her grandparents kept the boat for 36 years before passing it down to Robertson's parents in 1962. In 2001, Robertson became Sail Selina II's third steward.
"From the time I was about 12, even though I've got older siblings, everybody knew she would come to me," Robertson said. "I was the kid that was aboard, participating, had the interest."
Robertson made the decision to charter the boat so that she could afford to maintain it.
After Sail Selina II's final charter season, Robertson plans to pass the yacht down to her niece, who happens to live in Greenport, New York, where Sail Selina II was built.
"It's like a full-circle thing," Robertson said about the sailing yacht. "She's 100 years old. She's going back to the town she was built in."
Robertson said she knows her grandparents and father, who have since died, would be so proud of the boat's Chesapeake Gateways designation.
"I think they'd be tickled pink to know how much she has contributed to people's joy and experience over the last 25 years," Robertson said.
STEPPING ABOARDWith a 1,000-square-foot canvas sail, the 44-foot-long Sail Selina II is a "stable" and "regal" sailing yacht, Robertson said.
"We have a lot of guests that have never been on boats before, and they're a little bit nervous when they first step on," she said. "But by the time they get off, they go, 'Oh my God, this was like being on a flying magic carpet ride.'"
From wine and beer tasting cruises, to sunset sails, to engagement cruises, to weddings, to private sailing lessons, there are many options for those who want to set sail on Sail Selina II. Robertson said the standard two-hour tour takes passengers around St. Michaels Harbor before cruising out to the Miles River and putting up sails.
"We let the wind determine our course," Robertson said. "And before you know it, two hours has gone by."
Repeat passenger Gene Pisasale said he and his wife love sailing on Sail Selina II because they love being out on the water and they love sailing with Robertson.
"She's got to be the friendliest boat captain on the Chesapeake," said Pisasale, who lives in Pennsylvania. "And she is just a gem, a real gem. A pleasure to sail with."
To charter Sail Selina II during its last season, visit sailselina.com/ or call 410-726-9400. The season will go from April 18 through Nov. 2.

title: New director takes the helm at Chesapeake's Cambridge Center

New director takes the helm at Chesapeake's Cambridge Center

 August 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CAMBRIDGE - Dr. Lorelly Solano is combining her interests in education and public policy in her new role as director of the Chesapeake College Cambridge Center."I enjoyed working directly with the students - hearing about their dreams and learning about their challenges while I've helped them plan their academic journeys," Solano said. "This new role will be a bit different for me, but I will try to bring that student perspective into everything I do here." As director of the center, located on Race Street, Solano will lead the staff in providing all the services Cambridge-based students need to be successful. In the coming months, Cambridge residents are likely to meet Solano as she begins her community outreach efforts.The Cambridge Center, Solano said, is a resource for everyone in Dorchester County, playing a critical role in the economic and social health of the downtown area.In addition to credit classes in both transfer and career programs, the center also offers workforce training, personal enrichment opportunities and meeting spaces for community organizations. The center also houses the American Job Center."We're an education center for students of all ages, but I hope residents here also see us as a center of community growth," Solano said.Solano first joined Chesapeake as an English as a Second Language instructor.She was later the academic and career advisor guiding students through actionable plans to achieve their goals.A native of Costa Rica, Solano came to the United States as a graduate student.After earning her bachelor's degree in Costa Rica, she worked for an international flower exporter as she continued her studies toward licensure at the University of Costa Rica.Her future plans took a turn when a professor at UCR asked if she was adventurous.Thinking that the professor meant bungee jumping or some other daredevil sport, Solano prepared to decline. Instead, the professor asked if she would be interested in taking on a new academic challenge in a different country.He recommended her for a graduate research post at the University of Maryland.While working on "green" roof research and earning her master's degree in natural resources science at College Park, Solano's interest grew in building sustainable communities through policy and education.She went on to earn a Ph.D. in public policy and urban affairs at the University of Delaware."It's ironic that I studied urban affairs and ended up in rural area," Solano said. "Rural and urban areas face many of the same challenges, though, and people in both areas want the same things." Better lives and a greater sense of community, Solano said, are common desires for most people. The Cambridge Center provides both, she added.For more information about the Chesapeake College Cambridge Center, please visit www.chesapeake.edu/cambridge.

title: Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 941
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In the back of the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center on Race Street, one wall acts as a window into Tubman's life.Inside the museum, on one side of the wall, Tubman is painted as a young girl, about 13-years-old, at the Bucktown General Store.
"This was a pivotal time in her life," Linda Harris, the museum's director of events and docent, said. "It was considered her first act of defiance." Outside the museum, on the other side of the wall, Tubman is an adult, holding out her hand.
"(She's) coming back, rescuing family and those that wanted freedom," artist of both murals, Michael Rosato said.
Harriet Tubman, an abolitionist and social activist who was born into and escaped from slavery in Dorchester County in the 19th century, became well-known for her work on the Underground Railroad, a network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to their freedom.
Inside the museum, the mural of a young Tubman and the Bucktown Store covers the entire wall - and the other three walls in the room.
With canvas and paint, Rosato has transformed the back room of the museum into the Bucktown Store, a significant place in Tubman's history.
The story goes that Tubman was asked to go to the Bucktown Store to get something for the master.
"And she didn't want to do it," Bill Jarmon, president of the Harriet Tubman Organization, said.
"Part of it had to do with the fact that she wasn't presentable." It had to do with her hair, Jarmon said. So she covered her hair with a cloth made from flaxseed.
When Tubman got to the store, she heard a noise at the backdoor and saw a young boy struggling to get away from his master. When the boy escapes and runs toward the door, Tubman is told to stop him. But she doesn't. She steps out of the way to let him go through. "Her first act of defiance," as Harris said.
As the boy escaped, Jarmon said, a two-pound weight was thrown at him.
However, the weight hit Tubman in the forehead instead, knocking her unconscious.
Harris considers Tubman's head wrap to be a very important piece of this story.
"She wraps her head in this linen made of flaxseed, which in fact - what I'm reading and what I believe now - cushions the blow from that two-pound weight being hurled at her," Harris said.
"Imagine if she had fixed her hair that day. She'd be dead." Sitting in the back room of the museum Wednesday, Dec. 20, Jarmon and Harris pointed to different parts of the room as they told the story. When they officially open this part of the museum - which they hope to do in January - visitors will feel even more immersed in the story.
They plan to put in wood floors and counters to resemble the store. And as they tell the story of Tubman's first act of defiance, Harris said she and her husband will play code songs, songs enslaved people used to share messages.
Eventually, Harris hopes to offer virtual reality goggles to visitors when they enter the room.
"We're going to make this thing come alive," she said.
The idea to do this all started when Harris learned that she would no longer be able to take visitors on tours inside the original Bucktown Store.
Harris said that considering how pivotal the store was in Tubman's life, she couldn't have people visit and not learn the story.
"So I said, 'Well, let's put it in the museum,'" Harris said.
To begin the project, Rosato, who lives in Church Creek and has been an artist for 33 years, went to the store and took photos of the walls.
"Every square inch of the walls and what was on the shelves," he said.
After that, he took the photos back to his studio on Race Street and put paint to canvas.
"(I) just started to recreate the store as close as possible and in a somewhat realistic fashion so when you're in that space you feel as though you can take things off the shelves," he said.
After completing each wall on the canvas, he would bring the canvases to the museum and glue them to the walls so that it looked as if he had painted directly on walls of the museum. To make it look as realistic as possible, Rosato had to consider light, shadow and perspective.
"When you create a painting that you want to look real and dimensional, you have to understand perspective and find the right vanishing point," he said.
"So when you're standing right in the middle of that room, every wall you look at, all the lines converge to a certain point. And that's what gives it a sense of depth." The project, which Rosato worked on in the fall, took between one and two months to complete.
He said that once it is open to visitors, he hopes they will get a sense of the rich history of Tubman's experience in Dorchester County.
"The possibility of being able to stand there and reflect back like, 'I'm in the store where she is.
This is what happened,'" he said. "And then going outside and seeing (adult) Harriet Tubman. This is the outcome."

 CENTREVILLE — An overview of the pedestrian bridge plans to connect the Cross Island and South Island trails were presented to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners Nov. 26.In conjunction with the Parks and Recreation Department, Southern Kent Island Trail Extension Project staff obtained preliminary construction cost information for a pedestrian bridge crossing over MD Route 50, Chief Roads Engineer Shane Moore said.
Engineering consultant Kimley-Horn was contracted to complete a preliminary evaluation of several Route 50 pedestrian crossing locations east and west of the Route 8 overpass.
Utilizing the MDOT cost estimator to estimate a pedestrian crossing construction costs, As part of this evaluation Kimley-Horn estimated a pedestrian crossing construction cost at the Cracker Barrel location at $8.1 million, Moore said.
Construction only cost estimates were taken from similar type projects including Virginia's Tysons Old Meadow Pedestrian Bridge over Route 495 at $8 million and the Lane Place Pedestrian Bridge over Route 295 at between $10.8 and $12.4 million, according to Moore.
Several locations have been selected for a preliminary study through Kimley-Horn but there has been no final decision yet, according to Moore.
For safety, pedestrian bridges have to be built at a higher elevation than a typical vehicle overpass, Moore said.
With the commissioners' approval, Public Works staff will work with the BMC and RK&K Civil Engineering to develop a scope of services and costs for a final location study of the County's proposed MD Route 50 pedestrian bridge crossing.
Next steps include meeting with Maryland Transportation Authority and the State Highway Administration to begin discussions to nail down a final location for the construction of a pedestrian crossing, Moore said.
Queen Anne's County currently has about $120,000 in Baltimore Metropolitan Council (BMC) monies to be used for this study. In addition, BMC has also federally approved pre-established consulting contracts with RK&K, Moore said.

Caroline County Board of Ed declares last day of school, discuss virtual instruction

 EASTON — The Caroline County Board of Education declared Tuesday, June 17, as the last day of the extended school year after inclement weather closures exceeded the four days allotted.The last day will be a half day for students and a full day for teachers.
Next year, county schools will have three allotted inclement weather days. At the April 1 Board of Education meeting, district officials explored options for implementing virtual instruction should weather cause unexpected closures.
Because of the challenges presented by district officials, the board concluded it thinks the district will not be able to conduct virtual instruction on inclement weather days.
"The structure we tried to take with the presentation was a condensed version of some the requirements that the school system would have to meet if the county were to entertain virtual weather days," Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons said. "We walked through some real tough spots for us to get to those points."
Internet Connection and Google Meets
There are multiple factors Caroline County board of education most consider to conduct virtual inclement weather days. Including ensuring every student has a hotspot or wifi to participate in virtual learning.
Robert Wielgosz, supervisor of technology, led the discussion on cellular service, offering points on the Kajeet program.
Kajeet was a hotspot used during the pandemic for students to connect to the internet in areas where wifi access was limited and not available.
According to Wielgosz, when given the opportunity to use Kajeet, some students would use the hotspot for personal uses like video games and movies. This overloaded the hotspots and caused delays.
The estimate cost for Caroline County to provide the 700 needed Kajeet devices over five years would be about $736,000 for students and $35,000 for teachers.
Wielgosz also mentioned the need for Google Meet Breakout Rooms, which teachers use to conduct learning activities with groups in virtual classrooms. While this feature was available at no cost, it is no longer available in Caroline County's free Google plan.
"To get the feature back, it's going to cost Caroline County somewhere between $30,000 to $50,000 a year to get the premium Google aspect," Wielgosz said.
Multilingual Learners, Special Education and Homelessness
State law mandates districts "ensure that all staff and students, including students with disabilities, homeless students, and English language learners, have the necessary devices at home for virtual education days, including access to Wifi."
Providing equitable access to these services can be challenging during virtual instruction, district officials said.
Caroline County has 576 multilingual learners, 569 individualized education program students and 116 students who experience homelessness. For these students, hands-on teacher engagement and preparation is required for proper learning.
"It's very hard to keep students engaged, especially for four hours of synchronous instruction," Erica McDonald, supervisor of special education, said. "Without that in-person tangible motivating things that can keep them engaged during instruction, it can lead to increased frustration."
Providing necessary technologies and translation services are also complicated by virtual instruction, the officials said.
Teacher, staff negotiations
Some district employees work on inclement weather days, and some staff members do not work and still get paid, district officials said.
Requirements of the state say, "during virtual inclement weather days the local school system shall offer public school employees who are not assigned to work during the virtual education day an opportunity to make up the lost work through other duties before the beginning of the next school year."
The district would be responsible for determining how this work would be made up.
Virtual learning days require additional planning from teachers, which requires a negotiation with the teachers' union for proper pay.
"Our teachers work really hard. We all know are teachers work outside of hours. We have all come to accept that it comes with the job," Dr. Robert Willoughby, director of administrative services said. "However, the law does say that we may negotiate with our teachers' union. They have a right to come to negotiate if there is extra work here we would like extra compensation for that."
After going through the presentation, Simmons concluded it would be to hard for the county to pull off virtual inclement weather days.
"I don't see how as a county, with the resources we have right now, that this puts us in a great position to be able to hit all the marks to be able to pull this off effectively to meet all requirements," Simmons said.

 CHESTERTOWN - The lilting chorus of Cuban folk song "Guantanamera" filled the cafeteria of H.H.Garnet Elementary School in Chestertown Thursday, Sept. 21.Local resident and artist Fredy Granillo strummed his guitar as he taught the song to students that morning as part of the Celebración del mes del la Herencia Hispana in the county.The Celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month was brought into schools during September through partnerships with the Kent County Local Management Board and the Kent Cultural Alliance.The two organizations were joined by others in holding a variety of community events including art programs and a block party centered around Hispanic heritage."The Kent Cultural Alliance was honored to work with the Kent County Local Management Board and E(Ñ)E: Alianza para la Cultura y Comunidad Hispana, to create a month long celebration of the contributions of Kent County's Latino community," said John Schratwieser, executive director of the Kent Cultural Alliance."Celebrating those who contribute so much to our economic health and our quality of life, and doing that through art, music, food, dance and the written word, is paramount to the mission of the KCA." For Granillo, who also is a Kent County Public Schools parent, getting to share his family's cultural touchstones with students is a valuable experience.Granillo grew up in El Salvador. He and his wife Kent County Local Management Board Director Rosemary Ramsey Granillo moved to Chestertown when their son, a fourth grader at Garnet, was 2.Granillo found the community friendly and inviting, but he still faced hurdles - first being the language.He learned English and he helped his son with the language.There were additional cultural differences for Granillo as well, such as food, and he sees other families having similar experiences when they move here."I was lucky because I had the opportunity to visit Chestertown first," Granillo said. "So I knew about the artistic community in town and that was something that made me feel like I could live here." For students who move to Kent County from other countries, school can pose a big challenge.Beyond learning math standards, science, social studies and other subjects, they also have a new language to learn - and Kent County Public Schools has staff members dedicated to helping those English language learners.Granillo said programs like Hispanic Heritage Month are important for both students born and raised here and those who have moved to the area from other countries.It gives those students from other countries an opportunity and a space to share their culture with their new peers.Granillo spoke about how celebrations in other countries are often built around specific foods, activities and games - not unlike the American custom of eating turkey on Thanksgiving."I think it's really important for schools to have a space where these kids can show other kids what they like to do in their countries, because that gives you a perspective on the world," he said."When you are a kid, you need to understand the world is more than Chestertown or the town where you live." As part of Hispanic Heritage Month in Kent County Public Schools, there were lessons and school announcements teaching students about the culture.Galena Elementary School, for example, held a daily Hispanic Heritage contest, with questions that students could answer by looking at information posted throughout the building.Teacher Tracey Kendall-Parent works with local English language learners in Galena Elementary School. She took to the morning announcements throughout the month to provide information about countries where students' families are from."I think that's a beautiful experience for everybody, not just for the kids," Granillo said of the Hispanic heritage lessons. "And it's going to make these kids from other countries feel like they live in a space where they can celebrate their culture and their identity too."

title: White House OKs Maryland wind energy project
author: KATHARINE WILSON Capital News Service
content:
White House OKs Maryland wind energy project

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KATHARINE WILSON Capital News Service | Section: State News

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — Offshore wind energy is coming to Maryland, and with it, union jobs.The Biden administration on Thursday approved Baltimore-based US Wind's project to build offshore wind turbines about 10 miles off the coast of Ocean City, Maryland.
The offshore wind farm could generate over two gigawatts of wind energy and power over 718,000 homes, according to the Department of the Interior.
President Joe Biden said in a statement that the wind energy industry had been "struggling to gain a foothold" in the years before he came into office.
"From manufacturing and shipbuilding to port operations and construction, this industry will support tens of thousands of good-paying and union jobs, provide reliable clean power to homes and businesses, strengthen our power grid against outages, and help reduce pollution — all while protecting biodiversity and marine ecosystems," the president said.
Maryland Energy Administration Director Paul Pinsky called the Biden administration's action "an important step forward in the effort to bring clean, renewable energy production to Maryland's coast."
"Today's announcement underscores the careful, comprehensive and collaborative environmental analysis that has gone into these projects," Pinsky said in a statement.
The Maryland project is the tenth commercial-scale offshore wind energy project approved by the Biden administration. Combined, the projects are projected to generate 15 gigawatts of clean energy, half of Biden's goal of 30 gigawatts of offshore wind-produced energy by 2030.
The Maryland project includes up to 114 wind turbines, four offshore substation platforms and a meteorological tower. There will be three phases to the US Wind project, two of which — called MarWin and Momentum Wind — have already received offshore renewable energy certificates from the state.
Energy is set to start flowing in December 2028 from the first phase of the project. The final project is expected to be completed in late 2027 or early 2028, according to the plan submitted by US Wind.
The approval is a win for Maryland environmental groups and the state government, which have been working for offshore wind power in the state for around 10 years.
Starting in 2013, the Maryland legislature passed a series of bills to set offshore wind energy projects in motion.
The state set a goal in 2023, through the Promoting Offshore Wind Energy Resources Act, to generate 8.5 gigawatts of power from offshore wind by 2031.
This goal has hit some road bumps along the way, including the withdrawal of Denmark-based Ørsted's planned offshore wind projects in January.
US Wind won the competitive lease sale of the 46,970 acres of federal ocean waters in 2014.
"By moving away from reliance on dirty fossil fuel energy and building renewable energy, Marylanders will be able to breathe cleaner air and benefit from new clean energy jobs," Maryland Sierra Club Chapter Director Josh Tulkin said in a statement Thursday.
Jamie DeMarco, the federal campaigns coordinator for the Chesapeake Climate Action Network, said in an interview with Capital News Service that the Maryland wind farm is a milestone in moving offshore energy generation forward in Maryland.
"This is a huge undertaking to build an entire machine to deploy offshore wind, but once that machine is built, it'll be able to hum and crank out new domestic energy, and clean energy that's going to help us clean the air and meet our climate goals," DeMarco said.
Offshore wind turbines have been coming online across the East Coast, DeMarco said, but this will be the first operational offshore wind facility in Maryland.
Environmental advocates aren't the only celebrating parties. Union officials are touting the jobs set to be created by the wind farm.
Almost 2,680 jobs annually over seven years could be created during the development and construction phase of the wind farm, according to the Interior Department.
US Wind's planned permanent offshore wind components production facility, called Sparrows Point Steel in Sparrows Point, Baltimore — the former home of Bethlehem Steel — is forecast to generate jobs for steelworkers.
The Baltimore Bethlehem Steel mill, which closed in 2012, was once the largest steel producer in the world. Sparrows Point Steel will bring steelworker jobs back to Maryland, DeMarco said, in a way that hasn't been seen since the closure of Bethlehem.
Jim Strong, the offshore wind sector assistant for the United Steelworkers International Union, told CNS Thursday that the facility is expected to bring in over 500 jobs. The project will help not only steelworkers, Strong said, but other union trades as well.
"It's about addressing our climate crisis, about creating new green energy jobs — these will be high paid union jobs," Strong said.
Strong has served as a liaison between the union and US Wind. He said that the Sparrows Point facility has the opportunity to become a "central hub" for monopile production on the Atlantic Ocean. Monopiles, steel cylinders, are used for wind turbines, bridges and other projects, he said.
US Wind is a subsidiary of Italian company Renexia SpA.
The project has some detractors, like Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland), who represents the Eastern Shore.
"Offshore wind industrialization comes at a heavy cost to our marine life and environment, and is an incredibly expensive way to generate electricity," Harris said on X in July. "We should never allow foreign owned companies to control our energy supply — much less harm our environment while doing it."
The federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's director, Elizabeth Klein, said in a statement that the Maryland project "reflects the best available science and invaluable insights from Tribes, government agencies, local communities, industry leaders, ocean users, and environmental groups gathered during our extensive environmental review process."
"As we continue to support the undeniable momentum we see along our coasts, our focus remains on fostering responsible energy development, while protecting marine life and ecosystems," she said.
Democrats in the state, including Gov. Wes Moore, have been supportive of the project. Moore signed a memorandum of understanding with the federal government in June supporting offshore wind production.

title: GOP not there yet with articles of impeachment
author: Byron York
content:
GOP not there yet with articles of impeachment

 August 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Byron York | Page: A6 | Section: News 
 
 782
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's a lot of talk among House Republicans about impeaching President Joe Biden. But GOP members disagree on whether there is enough evidence to go forward.On one hand, Republican investigators have made enormous progress in the past few weeks. The testimony of former Hunter Biden business partner Devon Archer demolished Joe Biden's claim that he didn't talk to his son about Hunter's shady foreign business deals.GOP lawmakers are also finding increasing evidence that foreign money flowed to multiple members of the Biden family close to Joe Biden himself."We have caught Joe Biden in so many lies," House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer told Fox News recently. "I can't even count the number of lies now. So we have put together a case that I think would stand up in any court of law in America." Of course, no one is talking about criminal charges against the sitting president of the United States. Rather, if Republicans were to take action against Biden, it would be through impeachment.GOP House members have filed several resolutions of impeachment against Biden. Now there is a new one, the first since the Archer testimony, from a member of the House Judiciary Committee, Florida Republican Rep. Greg Steube. The resolution, containing four articles of impeachment, shows why the effort to impeach Biden is just not there yet.Article One attempts to link Joe Biden to Hunter Biden's, and brother James Biden's, influence peddling operations.The article says Hunter and James Biden "sold access" to then Vice President Joe Biden and then "sold promised access" to Joe Biden before he became president.Joe Biden himself "assisted by making appearances, phone calls, meeting with business partners, and knowingly allowing his family members to promise access to him and actions by him in furtherance of these schemes." The Biden family, the article says, benefited financially from that; Joe Biden's role was an "abuse of power" and a violation of federal law.Article Two accuses Joe Biden of obstruction of justice, charging that the Biden Justice Department interfered with investigations into Hunter Biden's activities. The accusations are taken from two IRS whistleblowers who have outlined in detail how DOJ dragged its feet and actually blocked IRS investigators from looking into what appeared to be clear tax evasion by Hunter Biden."These acts constitute an abuse of power as well as obstruction of justice," the article says.Article Three accuses Joe Biden of fraud for a matter in which James Biden allegedly deceived investors in a health care company. "Access to Joe Biden and indications that Joe Biden supported these schemes were used to lure investors into the schemes," the article says.Finally, Article Four accuses Joe Biden of "financial involvement in drug and prostitution activities." The article says Joe Biden and Hunter Biden "have a long history of comingled and intertwined finances." During the 2010s, Hunter Biden was famously blowing millions of dollars on drugs and prostitutes, both of which are illegal."Given the intermingled finances of Joe Biden and Hunter Biden, Joe Biden financially supported and should have been aware of these drug transactions and prostitution transactions," the article says. "Many of these transactions would have occurred using accounts with a nexus to Joe Biden." So that is the current case against Joe Biden. The obvious weakness in all the articles is that they are based on an effort to tie Joe Biden to Hunter Biden's, or James Biden's, allegedly illegal activities. Republicans have made great progress in beginning to discover such links. They have shown that Joe Biden lied about his knowledge of Hunter's activities, which is an important breakthrough. There appears to be much left to be discovered.In addition, Republican have convincingly established that the Biden administration improperly interfered with investigation of Hunter Biden's activities. That is an important breakthrough, too, although there is much more to learn.So as far as the first two articles are concerned, there is good reason for Republicans to push forward with their investigation. The third article, about James Biden, is very iffy, and the fourth article, about Joe Biden's knowledge of Hunter's drugging and whoring, will never go anywhere.And that is the current state of efforts to impeach Joe Biden. Republicans do not yet have a convincing case for impeachment. Maybe they will get there, and maybe they won't. As far as exercising general restraint against taking the extreme measure of impeachment is concerned - well, that sort of restraint went out with Nancy Pelosi's leadership of the House. If Republicans do eventually gather enough evidence against Biden, they'll use it. But they don't have it yet.Byron York is chief political correspondent for The Washington Examiner.COPYRIGHT 2023BYRON YORKDISTRIBUTED BY ANDREWS MCMEELSYNDICA TION

author: TALBOT COUNTY LIQUOR BOARD
content:
Talbot County Liquor Board license applications available

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TALBOT COUNTY LIQUOR BOARD | Section: Business 
 
 272
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The application process for the 2025-2026 Talbot County liquor licensing period is now available to the public.Businesses and individuals interested in applying for a new license, or renewing current licenses, can access the application on the board's webpage at talbotcountymd.gov/liquorboard.
All applications must be completed and submitted by March 31. Applicants are encouraged to review the application requirements and guidelines thoroughly to ensure compliance with local and state regulations.
In addition, in accordance with Talbot County Code, Article 2 — Alcoholic Beverages, "Renewal licenses shall be administratively approved without a hearing before the Board, unless a protest signed by not less than ten (10) residents or property owners in the voting district in which the place of business is located has been filed against the granting of a renewal license at least thirty (30) days before the expiration of the license for which renewal is sought." All protests for this license year must be filed on or before March 30, 2025. In the event a protest is filed, it shall be heard and determined as in the case of an original application."
All 2024-2025 alcoholic beverage licenses expire on April 30. The new license must be posted in the business by May 1.
"Our goal is to provide a streamlined and transparent process for applicants," said Victoria Bradley, secretary for the Talbot County Liquor Board. "We're here to assist individuals and businesses in navigating the application process successfully."
For questions or additional assistance, applicants can contact the Talbot County Liquor Board office at 410-770-8019 or via email at vbradley@talbotcountymd.gov. The office is open from 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday.

title: Lions tighten their grip on North
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Lions tighten their grip on North

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 754
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Noah Palmer offered somewhat of an explanation for his latest victory."My curveball," Queen Anne's County High's senior right-hander said with a game-winning smile. "I don't know what to say. I haven't been throwing it all year. It's been iffy. But I came out of the gate and it came out of my hand amazingly. And I was able to throw a split-finger today amazingly, too. I just threw it and it hit spots. That's all I got to say."
Palmer didn't have to say much more late Tuesday afternoon, as he yielded five hits in six-plus innings to help Queen Anne's to an 11-8 victory over Easton, drawing the Lions closer to their first North Bayside title since 1980.
Winners of five straight, Queen Anne's (8-6 overall, 5-1 North Bayside) can clinch the North championship with victories over Cambridge-South Dorchester and Kent County.
Colonel Richardson (11-5, 5-2), which blanked St. Michaels 3-0 yesterday behind Jordan Regulski's complete-game three-hitter, still remains in contention in the North. Should the Lions lose one of their two remaining division contests and finish tied with Colonel, the Colonels would win the North via their 8-1 victory over Queen Anne's in the only head-to-head meeting between the two schools this season.
Kent Island (7-8, 5-2) also has an outside shot. Though they lost to Queen Anne's in the second meeting between the two schools — which counts toward the division standings — the Bucs defeated Colonel and hold the tiebreaker between those two schools.
Easton (10-5, 4-3), which was in the running for its first North crown since 2007, got two first-inning runs against Palmer (5-2) but then was held scoreless by the Lions ace until the bottom of the sixth inning.
"Credit goes to their pitcher," Easton head coach Albert Pritchett said of Palmer, who struck out six and walked two before being relieved in the seventh. "He did a great job. After the first couple of innings he really settled in, working on his pitches, threw strikes."
Palmer and Easton's Kayden Webb (4-1) were locked in a pitcher's duel, tied at 2-2 heading to the top of the sixth.
That's when the Lions busted the game open, scoring six runs on five hits.
With one out, Noah Cramer walked, moved to second on a low pitch and scored the go-ahead run on Chance Hegedus' double down the left-field line. Ethan Keppler singled, sending Hegedus (3 for 4, three runs) to third. Hegedus got caught in a rundown between home and third. Warrior catcher Colin Mooney ran Hegedus back before throwing the ball to third baseman Garrett Fink. But with no one covering home, Hegedus raced across the plate for a 4-2 lead.
Webb was relieved after Brendan Parsley singled. Dustin Blue walked the first man he faced before Travis Sutch (4 for 4, three RBIs), whose solo homer off the left-field pole tied the game at 2-2 in the third, singled through the right side, plating two runs for a 6-2 lead. Two batters later, Dulin Clark belted a two-run double for an 8-2 lead.
"I think we're hitting pretty good right now," Travis Sutch said. "Definitely a big improvement over the last couple games. Everybody's starting to get going now, especially the bottom of our lineup."
Easton ended its scoring drought in the bottom of the sixth. Dylan Cassell doubled and scored when Blue sent a shot over Parsley's head in center field. Chase Raab's sacrifice fly made it 8-4. But Palmer got a strikeout and groundout to end the inning.
"He did a great job today," Queen Anne's head coach Rick Sutch said of Palmer. "He knew this was a big game. We went into it knowing that we were in the driver's seat as far as the Bayside North. He knew how big this was and he had at least five days off, so he was fresh.
"Usually Noah doesn't let anything bother him so once he got the lead I wasn't really too concerned," Coach Sutch added. "Webb's a good pitcher on the other side, so we knew we had to get to him early to get to the bullpen. But Noah did a great job. He controlled the game."
Queen Anne's tacked on three runs on five hits in the seventh, stretching their lead to 11-4.
The Warriors pieced together their biggest inning in the seventh, with Mikey O'Connor hitting a two-run single and Carter Mooney sending a sacrifice fly to center to make it 11-8 before Clough induced a game-ending groundout.
Notes: Webb tripled in the first and Colin Mooney doubled in the seventh for Easton.
